text.0_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: The word of Hashem that came to Hosea, etc., and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash: I have already explained in my commentary on Kings (II Kings 15) that from the time Joash conquered Amaziah, king of Judah, the kings of Judah were subordinate to the kings of Israel, and the kingdom was therefore designated by the names of the kings of Israel. This continued until the twenty-fourth year of Uzziah’s reign, which was the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam son of Joash. At that time Uzziah grew strong and reigned over an independent kingdom of his own, no longer subordinate to Jeroboam. With this you can understand why the prophecies of Hosea and Amos mention that they prophesied in the days of Jeroboam. Aside from the fact that we do not find any prophet identified by anything other than the kings of Judah among whom he prophesied, it would also be puzzling that, if the intention were to mention the kings of Israel who reigned during that period, why was only Jeroboam mentioned? After all, during those years Zechariah son of Jeroboam, Menahem, and Pekah also reigned over Israel. Rather, “in the days of Jeroboam” means before Uzziah grew strong enough to reign independently, when the entire kingdom was designated by the name of Jeroboam; and “in the days of Uzziah” means after the twenty-fourth year of his reign, from which time the kingdom was designated by the name of Uzziah. Since Uzziah’s rise to power occurred shortly before the earthquake, as I explained there in Kings, Amos as well—who prophesied two years before the earthquake—prophesied for approximately one year during the days of Jeroboam. Regarding Hosea, of whom it is stated simply that he prophesied in the days of Jeroboam—that is, while Jeroboam exercised general sovereignty over Judah as well—it may be presumed that this occurred several years earlier. In the prophecy of Isaiah, however, it is stated only that he prophesied in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, etc., without mentioning Jeroboam. It is therefore clear—even if we say that “in the year of King Uzziah’s death” (Isaiah 6) refers to the time when he became afflicted with leprosy—that Uzziah was already reigning independently. Consequently, Scripture does not mention that Isaiah prophesied in the days of Jeroboam. From this you can see how correct our Sages were in saying that Hosea was the first to prophesy among the four prophets who lived in his time, even if we do not interpret “the beginning of Hashem’s speaking through Hosea” as meaning that he was the first of the four prophets who lived in his time.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: The beginning of Hashem’s speaking through Hosea: The expression “speaking through,” in which the verb “to speak” is followed by the letter bet, refers to the Divine Spirit speaking through the prophet for the prophet’s own sake, rather than for the purpose of a mission to the people as a whole. It also denotes speech expressing complaint and displeasure. From this our Sages inferred that this was the first communication of the Divine Spirit to Hosea; that Hashem engaged him in a certain dispute; and that this communication involved a complaint. That is to say, at the beginning of Hashem’s speaking with Hosea, He disputed with Hosea and expressed displeasure toward him. From this dispute it came about that Hashem said to Hosea, “Go, take for yourself a wife of harlotry.” Presumably, the dispute concerned the command that followed it. Our Sages expounded that Hashem told Hosea that Israel had sinned, and Hosea replied, “Exchange them for another nation.” Hashem answered that He could not exchange them, because they were His children. He therefore commanded Hosea to take a harlot as a wife. After she bore him children, He commanded him to divorce her. Hosea replied, “How can I divorce her? I have children by her!” Through this Hashem demonstrated to him that He likewise could not divorce Israel. Hosea then retracted his words and blessed them. This was the answer to the dispute in which Hashem told him that Israel had sinned: He wished Hosea to go on a mission to rebuke them and restore them to the proper path, for this responsibility rests upon the prophets, as it later says, “Contend with your mother, contend.” Hosea did not wish to undertake the mission of prophesying to them and rebuking them. He told Hashem not to attempt to restore them to the proper path, because after they had strayed after foreign gods, He ought to treat them as a man treats a wife who has committed harlotry: her husband sends her away from his house and never returns to her. Hashem said to him: “If so—since you do not wish to rebuke them and restore them to the proper path, while I do not wish to send them away because I also have righteous children among them—then be like Me, and take for yourself a wife of harlotry,” meaning a woman publicly known for harlotry, and children of harlotry, meaning that she already had children whom she had borne through harlotry, which constituted evidence that she was a harlot, as it says, “Tamar, your daughter-in-law, has committed harlotry, and moreover, behold, she is pregnant through harlotry.” Alternatively, as some commentators explain, the children she would bear to Hosea would be suspected of having been conceived through harlotry. For the land shall surely stray from following Hashem: Thus, the congregation of Israel is a wife who commits harlotry by pursuing idolatry, and the children whom she bears are born in harlotry, possessing thoughts of heresy and idolatry like their fathers. Nevertheless, I continue to keep her as My wife, and so shall you do. The commentators found it difficult to understand how Hashem could have commanded the prophet to take a harlot as his wife. Ibn Ezra therefore says that this occurred only in a prophetic vision, while Targum Jonathan explains it allegorically. But there is no necessity for either interpretation, for Hosea was not a priest, and a harlot is not forbidden in marriage to an ordinary Israelite. Moreover, we find that Hashem commanded prophets to perform acts that were not ordinarily proper according to the laws of the Torah, as temporary rulings required by the occasion. Thus, He commanded Ezekiel to shave the corners of his head and his beard with a razor, and Elijah offered a sacrifice during the period when private altars were forbidden.
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: So he went and took Gomer daughter of Diblaim: Our Sages explained that she was so named because everyone would finish with her and trample her like a cake of pressed figs. That is, the Children of Israel were compared to figs, as it says (Jeremiah 24:1), “Hashem showed me, and behold, there were two baskets of figs.” A fig begins to spoil immediately after it ripens, unless it is dried and made into a cake of pressed figs, in which case it is preserved. Their ancestors resembled a cake of pressed figs that had shriveled in the sun so that it would not spoil. She, however, was like gomer—a fig that had fully ripened but had not been dried, and therefore spoiled. She conceived and bore him a son: The first son was still regarded as specifically his, for he had been fathered by him. He therefore did not give him a name expressing hatred toward him, but only the name Jezreel. This is because the earlier generations, although they had strayed through the sin of Jeroboam, still worshiped Hashem in conjunction with other powers and were therefore still associated with Hashem. This son represents all the generations from the days of Jehu until the end of the reign of Jehu’s dynasty. Although the woman was a wife of harlotry, her children were nevertheless still associated with Hashem; for although Jehu did not depart from the sin of Jeroboam, he abolished the worship of Baal and believed in Hashem. To them, the calves represented a kind of worship in conjunction with God, or intermediaries through which spiritual influence and Divine bounty were brought down.
text.0_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Call his name Jezreel: He explains the reason: for yet a little while—within a few days—and I will visit the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu. That is, the punishment and vengeance that I carried out against the house of Ahab in the portion of Jezreel because it practiced idolatry—which punishment is called “the bloodshed of Jezreel”—I will visit upon the house of Jehu as well, because they too practiced idolatry. And I will bring an end to the kingdom of the house of Israel: This refers to the kingdom of the house of Jehu, which had already become an established dynasty, for it continued through four generations, and Jeroboam had restored the border of Israel to its former extent, as stated in II Kings 14. I will bring this kingdom to an end through the killing of Zechariah son of Jeroboam.
text.0_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be on that day: On the day of reckoning, I will break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel. This may be interpreted as referring to the dynasty of Jehu in general, which Jehu seized by means of the bow when he triumphed in the Valley of Jezreel. There Jehu drew his bow and struck Jehoram, thereby taking possession of the kingdom, as stated in II Kings 9:24; therefore, Hashem says, “I will break the power of that bow.” Alternatively, it may refer to the bow that Elisha gave to Joash, king of Israel, with which to shoot arrows that would be arrows of deliverance through which he would defeat Aram. By means of that bow he defeated Aram and strengthened his kingdom. The power of the house of Jehu is therefore represented by this bow. I will break it through the judgment associated with the Valley of Jezreel, where He had determined to execute judgment against those who practiced idolatry.
text.0_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: She conceived again and bore a daughter: Through this he represents the kings who arose after the kingdom of Jehu had come to an end. They were weak kings, as indicated by the image of a daughter. Here it does not say, “and she bore him a daughter,” because by then she had already begun committing harlotry with other men, and he was uncertain whether the daughter had been born to him. In the allegory, during these generations the number of righteous people diminished even further, and they all corrupted their conduct by straying after idolatry. He said to him, “Call her name Lo-Ruhamah”: This name signifies, for I will no longer have compassion upon the house of Israel, that I should surely forgive them and pardon their sins. That is, although in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash Hashem had compassion upon Israel, forgave their sin, and delivered them—as it says (II Kings 14:26), “For Hashem saw the affliction of Israel,” etc., “and Hashem had not said that He would blot out the name of Israel, so He delivered them through Jeroboam son of Joash”—He would now no longer continue to have compassion upon them or forgive them, for He would exile them. Through the name Lo-Ruhamah, the prophet had already displayed hatred toward his daughter and his wife. Nevertheless, he did not yet call her “Lo-Ammi,” a name signifying that the bond between him and them had been severed entirely. For although He would not have compassion upon the Ten Tribes, they were still His people because Judah and Benjamin, together with the tribes that had joined them, still remained. Concerning this he says:
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: But I will have compassion upon the house of Judah and save them through Hashem: For Hezekiah and his people were saved through Hashem and were delivered from Sennacherib by a miracle. I will not save them by bow, etc., for an angel of Hashem went forth and struck the Assyrian camp. For this reason, they still remain My people, and the mother remains My wife.
text.0_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: When she had weaned Lo-Ruhamah: She did not give birth to the third child immediately, during the nursing of the second, as she had given birth to the second child soon after the first. Rather, only after she had weaned Lo-Ruhamah did she conceive the third child. This third child, who was called Lo-Ammi, represents the destruction of Judah and its exile, which did not occur immediately but only after many years had passed. She conceived and bore a son: For the kingdom of Judah was a powerful kingdom in the days of Hezekiah and Josiah, and it is therefore represented by a male child.
text.0_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: He said, “Call his name Lo-Ammi”: He then commanded Hosea to give him a name signifying that he was not his son at all, and consequently that the mother was not his wife. For when a father says to his son, “You are not my people,” the bond between him and his wife is also severed, since she has borne children through harlotry. He explained the reason to him: for you are not My people, and I will not be for you as a father, husband, or master. Our Sages therefore said that He commanded Hosea to divorce his wife, as indicated by the name Lo-Ammi. Hashem would then do likewise: divorce Israel and exchange them for another nation.
text.1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be—Hosea’s response: Hosea was distressed at the thought of divorcing his wife and abandoning his children. He therefore withdrew his earlier words and began to plead Israel’s cause. He said to Hashem: “How can You wish to send away the mother—the congregation of Israel—and her children? In the future, the number of the Children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which can neither be measured nor counted.” That is, although the grains of sand have a finite number—for it has already been explained that the actual existence of an infinite multitude is impossible (as stated in the Guide for the Perplexed, Part II)—nevertheless, even though they have a number, no person can count them because of their vast quantity and minuteness. Although it would theoretically be possible to measure the sand by volume, this too cannot be done, because much of it lies concealed in the depths of the sea and the abysses of the earth, places that human beings cannot reach. Likewise, it will be impossible to count Israel, both because of their great multitude and because they will be scattered and hidden at the ends of the earth. Thus, many of the tribes will be considered lost, since no one knows their location, like sand concealed in the depths of the seas. Then, in the place where Hashem has now commanded that it be said to them, “You are not My people”—that is, in the place to which He banished them in exile and concealed His face from them—it shall be said to them that they are children of the living God. At that time everyone will recognize that their Father lives and watches over His children with a unique and wondrous Providence, through which they will have endured throughout the long period of exile. Their descendants will become known among the nations as offspring blessed by Hashem.
text.1_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And they shall be gathered together: Then, at the End of Days, the scattered exiles shall be gathered—both the children of Judah, who were exiled by Nebuchadnezzar at the destruction of the First Temple and did not all return in the days of Ezra, and the children of Israel, the Ten Tribes who were exiled by the king of Assyria. They shall all be gathered from the places of their dispersion and shall be together as one people. They shall also appoint for themselves one leader, namely Messiah son of Joseph, who will initially serve as their leader (as stated in Ezekiel, chapter 37). And they shall ascend from the land: They shall ascend from throughout the earth, across which they have been scattered, to the Land of Israel. For great shall be the day of Jezreel: At that time, the name of the first son, Jezreel, which had indicated Hashem’s judgment against them, shall be fulfilled in a different sense, as it says (verse 25), “I will sow her for Myself in the land.” He shall be called Jezreel in the sense of sowing. The exile will resemble the sowing of kernels of grain deep within the earth: it appears that the kernels have rotted and decayed, but afterward they sprout, grow, and yield many times their number in grain. Likewise, from the exiles who were sown throughout the lands there shall sprout a people as numerous as the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted, together with the converts who join them, as our Sages taught. “The day of Jezreel” means the day on which this sowing—the people whom God sowed in the earth—will become manifest and bear its sheaves. That day will be exceedingly great because of the miracles and mighty deeds that Hashem will perform on that day before the eyes of all the nations.
text.1_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Say: That is, since the number of the Children of Israel shall become like the sand of the sea, etc., I therefore command the sons and the daughter: Say to your brothers—whom they sought to call Lo-Ammi, “Not My People”—that they are Ammi, “My People,” and to your sisters—whom they sought to call Lo-Ruhamah, “Not Pitied”—that they are Ruhamah, “Pitied.” For in the future they will be Hashem’s people, and Hashem will have compassion upon them. Through this, Hosea argued against Hashem’s wish that he send away his wife and call his children Lo-Ruhamah and Lo-Ammi, and he asks that Hashem likewise say to them, “You are My people,” in view of what they will become in the future.
text.1_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Contend: This is Hashem’s response: If so, you, the children, must contend with your mother and rebuke her for her harlotry. For as long as she is not My wife but strays from Me in harlotry, I am not her Husband, and the children are not Mine. It therefore rests upon you, the children, to contend with your mother so that she will correct her ways. This is Hashem’s answer to Hosea: If so, it is the duty of the prophets—including Hosea—to contend with the mother, meaning the congregation of Israel, to rebuke her and restore her to the proper path. Let her remove: Contend with her that she remove her harlotry from her face—the idolatry that she practices publicly, so that the signs of her harlotry are visible upon her face—and her adulteries from between her breasts—the desire for adultery itself, concealed between her breasts, namely the inclination toward idolatry and the inclination toward sexual immorality.
text.1_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Lest: If she does not remove her harlotry from her face, then, since she is not My wife and I am not her Husband, as stated above, I will strip her naked and take from her the garments that I gave her. The prophet portrays the condition of the people when Hashem chose them in Egypt as that of an abandoned infant girl whose parents cast her naked into the wilderness, wallowing in her blood. Hashem passed by her, washed away her blood, clothed her, took her as His wife, and brought her into an inhabited city and a land flowing with milk and honey, as stated in Ezekiel 16: “On the day you were born, your navel cord was not cut,” etc.; “I passed by you and saw you wallowing in your blood,” etc.; “You were naked and bare”; “I spread My wing over you and covered you”; “I clothed you in embroidered garments,” etc. Accordingly, He says that once her harlotry causes the marriage to be annulled, I will strip her naked, as she had formerly been naked and bare. More than this, I will make her as she was on the day she was born, when she lay wallowing in her blood, and I will make her like a wilderness, a parched land, until she dies of thirst. That is, I will return her to exile among the nations, which is represented by the wilderness. There she will wallow in the blood of the slain, and I will take from her the garments I had given her—the indwelling of the Divine Presence, Divine Providence, and all the adornments of her glory.
text.1_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And upon her children: Consequently, I will not have compassion upon her children either. In the allegory, I will not spare even the righteous among them, for since the congregation as a whole has strayed from Me in harlotry, the world is judged according to the majority, and they too are children of harlotry.
text.1_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: For their mother has committed harlotry: Therefore, her children are children of harlotry. Although one might argue that most acts of intercourse are presumed to be with the husband, and that even if the mother committed harlotry her children remain legitimate, nevertheless, she who conceived them has brought shame upon them: she has cast disgrace upon her children’s conception to the point that their legitimacy is doubtful. For she said, “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water”: The principle that most acts of intercourse are presumed to be with the husband applies only when she commits harlotry in secret, remains under her husband’s authority, and is supported at his table. In that case, he remains her primary partner, and most of her relations are with him. But she has already separated from her husband: first, because she openly publicizes her harlotry, declaring publicly, “I will go after my lovers,” and leaves his authority for that of her paramours; and second, because according to her own words, she is no longer supported by her husband but receives her provisions from her paramours. They provide my bread and my water, and likewise her clothing: they provide my wool and my flax, from which she spins garments for herself. They also supply her remaining needs: oil for anointing herself, and drinks, such as wine and milk, for her enjoyment. Consequently, most of her relations are with her paramours, and her children are indeed children of harlotry. In the allegory, the congregation of Israel has separated itself from Hashem entirely and practices idolatry openly. It believes that all its abundance and success come from the configurations of the stars and constellations, that Hashem neither does good nor causes harm, and that serving Him provides no benefit whatsoever. Through this, Israel has become like all the families of the earth, serving wood and stone. Hashem will therefore have no compassion even upon the good among them, but will cast them all away from His presence.
text.1_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, behold, I will hedge up your way with thorns: This describes the efforts Hashem will make to bring her back to Him, by comparison to the measures a husband would take toward a wife who commits adultery against him. She has a broad, established road by which she leaves his house each day to go to her lovers, so he blocks the road with thorns to prevent her from traveling upon it. Yet she still has a place behind the fence where she can speak with her lovers through an opening in it; therefore He says, and I will wall up her wall. She still has narrow, private paths by which she can go out to them, so He says that He will destroy those paths so that she will no longer find her paths. In this way, He will confine her and separate her from those who commit harlotry with her. In the allegory, Hashem will alter the order and governance of the celestial systems and surround Israel with a barrier so that they cannot bestow goodness and prosperity upon her. He will frustrate all the practices, mystical devices, and talismans she employs in an attempt to draw down their influence and blessing. He will also create hostility between her and the neighboring nations in whom she trusted to come to her aid, whose practices she learned, and with whom she made covenants. He will close her in so that she cannot go out to them, associate with them, or intermingle with them.
text.1_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And she shall pursue: Besides preventing her from going out, He will also cause her lovers to distance themselves from her. At first, she will pursue them but will not overtake them, because they will flee from her. Afterward, they will disappear from her sight entirely, so that when she seeks them, she will not find them. In the allegory, the prosperity she attributed to nature and the celestial order will distance itself from her until it disappears from her sight and she no longer knows where it can be found. Likewise, the assistance and alliances she had with the surrounding nations will be taken from her. Then she will say, “I will go and return to my first Husband, for it was better for me then than now.” Although necessity will compel her to return to Me, she will nevertheless fail to recognize her sin. Rather, she will resemble the adulterous woman described above: even after her lovers distance themselves from her, and she pursues them but can no longer find them, until she is finally forced to return to her husband’s house, she will not regret her conduct or her harlotry. On the contrary, she will lament that she is compelled to return to her husband’s house. She will explicitly say: “My decision to go and return to my first Husband is not because I regret leaving his house for the house of my lovers, nor because life with my Husband was better than life with them. On the contrary, life with my lovers was better than life with my Husband. I am returning only because it was better for me then than now—compared with my present condition, in which my lovers have abandoned me and I now have no helper or supporter, my former condition in my husband’s house was better. Yet it was still not as good as my condition when I lived with my lovers, who provided my bread and my water, for then I was better off than in my husband’s house.” In the allegory, even after Israel’s prosperity has vanished and many evils and afflictions have befallen her, compelling her to repent, she will imagine that this occurred because the celestial order and her fortune have turned against her and placed her beneath an unfavorable constellation. After employing every device and form of foreign worship in pursuit of her lovers, seeking to restore the favorable influence of the celestial order, all without success, she will be compelled to return to Hashem and seek refuge beneath the shelter of Divine Providence. Yet she will say that sheltering beneath Divine Providence is preferable only in comparison with her present condition, in which the celestial order opposes her—not in comparison with a time when it looks favorably upon her, for then she would be prepared to return to her lovers and resume her foreign worship.
text.1_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: But she did not know: This resulted from her failure to understand that even at first, when she practiced idolatry and possessed every good thing, these did not come from her lovers or from the influence of the stars. Rather, it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil. This indicates that even now she still believes in idolatry and imagines that the prosperity she formerly enjoyed came from the influence of the stars and from idolatrous worship. She does not realize that Israel is not subject to the celestial order, and that all the abundance she enjoyed came through Divine Providence: it was Hashem who gave her the grain and wine. Yet they denied Hashem’s goodness, even when He greatly increased the benefits He bestowed upon her through His Providence, to the point that I multiplied silver and gold for her, which they used for Baal. They fashioned Baal from My silver and My gold, which I had given her; Baal had given her nothing. Thus, all the prosperity she had enjoyed until now came through Divine Providence, while the adversity now befalling her results from Divine Providence having been withdrawn from her. Therefore, the earth has withheld its produce and the heavens have been restrained.
text.1_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, I will return: Hashem said that He would therefore act toward them in ways that would lead them to recognize that the withholding of their prosperity and the adversity befalling them came not from the celestial order but through Divine Providence. Until then, when He had restrained the heavens from sending rain, they imagined that this had resulted from nature and the celestial order and did not recognize that Hashem had caused it all. He will therefore do the opposite: He will send rain upon the earth, and the earth will yield its produce, so that they will see that according to nature and the celestial order they are prepared to receive goodness and blessing, and that grain and bread should be plentiful in the land. Yet precisely when the grain and wine have fully ripened, Hashem will return and take them away. Thus He says, therefore, I will return and take away My grain in its season: When the grain has ripened at harvest time, I will return and take it back, and through this they will recognize that their adversity has come through Divine Providence. Likewise, I will rescue My wool and My flax, which have already been produced and are ready to cover her nakedness; I will rescue them from her possession and take them from her. She will then see that although her lovers—the stars of the celestial order and the processes of nature—are prepared to assist her and bestow good upon her, they will nevertheless be unable to help her or rescue her from the hand of Hashem. Thus He says:
text.1_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And now I will expose her disgrace before the eyes of her lovers: Although her lovers—the forces of the celestial order—stand beside her and look favorably upon her, I will nevertheless strip away her garments and expose her disgrace. No one shall rescue her from My hand. Through this she will understand that they possess no power against Hashem. Not only are they incapable of giving her anything without Hashem’s will, but they cannot even enable her to retain the prosperity she has already obtained.
text.1_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will cause to cease: This is the second measure: I will cause all her rejoicing to cease—her festivals and her new moons, when she celebrated with foreign worship, believing that these appointed times were auspicious days during which the stars would bestow prosperity and blessing. I will abolish those joyful occasions by transforming them into days of distress and darkness. From this she will recognize that goodness and happiness do not depend upon the celestial order but upon Hashem, who changes the times and arranges the stars in their stations according to His will.
text.1_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will lay waste her vine and her fig tree: This is the third measure. He will not merely withhold the produce of the land but will also lay waste the land itself and its choicest fruit-bearing trees—the vine and the fig tree—because she said, “These are my payment, which my lovers have given me.” She attributed even her inheritance of the land to the Baals, like a harlot who brazenly claims that the dowry her husband gave her was payment she received from her lovers. I will therefore lay waste the fruit-bearing trees and turn them into a forest, where the wild beasts gather and consume their fruit. In the allegory, the wild nations whom Sennacherib settled there will gather in the land and consume the fruit of Israel’s vines and fig trees. The meaning of all this is that after she said, “I will go and return to my first Husband”—referring to the time when the people began to return somewhat during the reign of Hoshea son of Elah, who abolished the guards stationed by the kings of Israel to prevent the people from making the pilgrimage to Jerusalem—Hashem saw that their repentance was not complete and that their hearts still inclined toward idolatry. They returned only because they believed that their fortune had turned against them. Hashem therefore brought the king of Assyria against them, repeatedly devastated their land, and allowed foreigners to dispossess them.
text.1_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will visit: He says that in the end, He saw that all the measures He had taken to make her recognize that the adversity befalling her was a punishment imposed through Divine Providence had accomplished nothing. For I saw that when I visited upon her the days of the Baals, to which she burned incense, punishing them for this, she did not thereby return to Me. Instead, she adorned herself with her nose-ring and her jewelry and went after her lovers. She resembled a harlot whose husband stripped her of all her clothing and took away all her ornaments so that she could not go after her paramours. Yet when she was left with only a single nose-ring and one piece of jewelry, she adorned herself with those remaining ornaments in order to go after her lovers. Likewise, even when Hashem punished them in the days of Hoshea son of Elah and the king of Assyria took away everything they possessed, they did not return to Hashem. Instead, they sent to So, king of Egypt, and persisted in the worship of foreign gods. But Me she forgot: Therefore, she did not return to Hashem who had struck her, but sought assistance from foreign nations and deliverance through the worship of foreign gods.
text.1_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, behold, I will entice her and lead her into the wilderness: He compares her to a harlot whose husband sees that none of the measures he has taken to separate her from her paramours has succeeded. He therefore entices her away from the inhabited region, where her paramours are found, and leads her into the wilderness, where she will find no man with whom to commit harlotry and will be alone with her husband. There I will speak to her heart to restore her love for Me. By this he refers to what is stated in Ezekiel 20:35: “I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face.” This refers to the exiles into which Israel will be driven among the nations. Although they will dwell among the nations, they will be as though in a desolate wilderness, for the nations will distance themselves from them. They will be hungry and thirsty, surrounded by snakes and scorpions that sting them. There it also says, “I will bring you into the bond of the covenant,” etc. This is what is meant by His leading them into the wilderness: there they will be under Hashem’s Providence, and there He will speak to their hearts so that they return to Him.
text.1_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will give her vineyards to her from there: The vineyards that He took from them, as it says, “I will lay waste her vine and her fig tree,” He will give back to them from there. The metaphor is that there the husband will resume loving his wife, once she is faithful to him, and will restore the vineyards he had taken from her because of her harlotry. In the allegory, He compares her condition to the time of her departure from Egypt, when He brought them into the wilderness. There they received the Torah and the true faith, came under His special Providence, and witnessed His signs and deeds. There her paramours are absent, for the celestial order cannot bestow prosperity in the desolate, howling wilderness. According to nature, there is neither bread nor water there, much less vines and fig trees. Yet “I will give her vineyards to her” means that I will provide her sustenance and all her needs. During their exile, they should naturally lack every good thing, since they were prevented from purchasing fields and vineyards and from acquiring livestock and property. Only through Hashem’s wondrous Providence will a remnant survive and obtain all that it needs. He also refers to the spiritual vineyards—the Torah and the faith—for which they sacrificed their lives in exile during periods of slaughter and forced conversion. These are the vineyards of which Scripture speaks in the Song of Songs, when it says, “My own vineyard I did not keep,” as I explained there. Ultimately, I will give her the Valley of Achor as an entrance to hope: At the End of Days, He will relieve the severity of their subjugation. They will find favor and kindness wherever they are exiled and will begin to hope for freedom and redemption. And she will respond there as in the days of her youth: The miracles performed for them in former times will return. “The days of her youth” alludes to the miracles they experienced in ancient days, such as during the conquest of the Land and the building of the Temple in the days of Solomon; and as on the day she ascended from the land of Egypt refers to the miracles performed for them in Egypt and at the Red Sea.
text.1_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be on that day, declares Hashem, that you will call Me “my Husband”: The term baal denotes dominion and ownership: one exercises authority over something because it belongs to him and is his possession. The term ish, however, denotes love, closeness, and the marital relationship. Until now, when Hashem had no closeness with them and His Providence was hidden and veiled behind the natural order, they served Him out of fear and called Him Baali, “my Master,” because of His dominion over them. In such a relationship, they would sometimes turn toward His servants—the intermediaries through whom the bounty coming from Him reached them—and would fear and honor them as well. In the future, however, He will walk among them and bestow His blessings upon them without any intermediary, just as a man unites with his wife. This is what our Sages meant when they said that she will be like a bride in her father-in-law’s house, rather than like a bride in her father’s house. For His dwelling will be in the lower world, where His glory will reside among them. She will receive the Divine bounty face to face, serve Him out of love, and neither fear nor honor any being besides Him.
text.1_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will remove: Consequently, I will remove the names of the Baals from her mouth, for she will no longer acknowledge intermediaries that convey bounty and blessing to her from her exalted Husband. Moreover, they shall no longer be mentioned by name, for the entire world will then be governed by Hashem’s Providence rather than by the celestial order, until the worship of the Baals is abolished entirely.
text.1_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will make a covenant for them on that day with the beasts of the field: The celestial order and nature will no longer rule over human beings, but only over the beasts and birds, which will remain subject to the governance of nature, whereas human beings will not, as Don Isaac Abarbanel explains. According to its literal meaning as well, it says that no evil will then be found in the world. There will be no harm from creatures that act according to instinct, for He will make a covenant with the wild beasts so that they do not injure anyone. This also serves as a metaphor for savage people, like beasts of prey, who devoured Israel in earlier times. Nor will there be evils caused by beings possessing free choice, for I will break bow, sword, and warfare from the earth. Consequently, I will cause them to lie down securely. Similarly, it says in Ezekiel 34, “I will make a covenant of peace with them and eliminate wild beasts from the land, and they shall dwell securely in the wilderness.” Likewise, among the promises given by the master of the prophets, it says (Leviticus 26:6), “I will eliminate wild beasts from the land, and no sword shall pass through your land.”
text.1_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will betroth you to Me: Then I will betroth you anew, as it says, “As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.” This new betrothal will differ from the former one, as it says, “I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel.” The earlier betrothal was only temporary, for they were destined to sin and thereby dissolve the bond, as it says, “When you beget children and grandchildren,” etc., “you shall quickly and utterly perish,” etc. Similarly, it says, “This people will rise and stray after foreign gods,” etc., “and My anger will burn against them,” etc. At that future time, however, they will no longer sin, and the bond will never be dissolved. Thus He says, I will betroth you to Me forever. This will occur because I will betroth you to Me with righteousness and with justice. Human perfection depends upon two kinds of conduct: first, matters between one person and another; and second, matters between a person and God. Concerning matters between one person and another, He says that they will then practice righteousness and justice. Justice means acting according to the strict requirements of the law, while righteousness means acting beyond the strict requirements of the law. Because you will bring as your dowry two precious qualities—righteousness and justice—the One who betroths you will correspondingly give you two precious gifts: kindness and compassion. One who acts with compassion considers the suffering and affliction of the recipient and treats him as is fitting; this corresponds to justice. One who acts with kindness does not consider whether the recipient is deserving, but acts toward him solely from the quality of his own kindness; this corresponds to the righteousness that they will practice.
text.1_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will betroth you: Regarding the commandments between a person and God, their foundation depends upon faith—believing in Hashem, His Torah, and His promises. Therefore He says, I will betroth you to Me in faith. After the betrothed woman brings this gift of faith in her hand, He will give her a corresponding gift from His side: and you shall know Hashem. He will reveal to her His signs and wonders and cause His Divine Presence to dwell among them, until they know Hashem with clear knowledge, like something apprehended by the senses. They will no longer require faith, for faith concerns something of which a person has no clear knowledge and accepts only through tradition. They, however, will possess knowledge of Hashem, which is greater than faith.
text.1_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be on that day that I will answer, declares Hashem: In his figurative language, the prophet depicts the seed sown in the earth as asking and making a request of the grain, wine, and oil. The seed’s request is that it produce a crop and that grain, wine, and oil grow from what was sown. The grain, wine, and oil in turn ask and make a request of the earth, for they seek that the earth give them its strength and nourish them with its moisture, richness, and fertile essence. The earth asks and makes a request of the heavens, that they provide abundant rain—the early and latter rains in their proper seasons—as well as the precious produce brought forth by the sun and the yield brought forth by the moons. The heavens then ask and make a request of Hashem, who sends rain in its season according to His Providence and decree. For although rain may be due according to nature, it is sometimes withheld by a decree of Divine Providence, as it says, “I also withheld the rain from you when there were still three months until the harvest.” At the present time, the grain, wine, and oil sometimes fail to answer the seed, as when blight, mildew, locust, or caterpillar destroys the produce of the land. Sometimes the earth fails to answer the grain and wine because the soil’s fertility has been ruined, as it says, “When you cultivate the ground, it shall no longer yield its strength to you.” Sometimes the heavens fail to answer the earth because natural conditions bring drought and dryness, and no rain falls. At other times, Hashem does not answer the heavens, withholding rain through Divine Providence so that no rains of blessing descend. At that future time, however, each will answer the one that asks of it, and everything required will be supplied for all their needs. This will result from the universal providential response that comes from Hashem. Therefore He says, “And it shall be on that day that I will answer, declares Hashem.” Through this, all four entities mentioned will be moved to provide the proper response. First, the response of Divine Providence will come to the heavens. Thus He says, I will answer the heavens: He will command them to pour forth providential rain from His providential blessing. And they will answer the earth: The heavens and the arrangements of the celestial order will also accord with the blessing, so that He will not need to overturn or disrupt nature, for they will be prepared to answer the earth and grant its request.
text.1_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And the earth shall answer the grain: The earth’s strength and fertile richness will increase, enabling it to fulfill the request of the grain and the wine by causing them to yield abundant produce.
text.1_Chapter, 23_Verse, 1_Comment: And they shall answer Jezreel: They will fulfill the request of the seed that was sown, enabling it to bear a crop.
text.1_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will sow her for Myself in the land: He now explains that the metaphor describing a response coming from Hashem and descending from one level to the next, until the grain and wine answer Jezreel, also refers figuratively to the sowing of the house of Israel. This will signal that the names of all three children mentioned in chapter 1 are to be transformed for the good. The name of the first son, Jezreel, had indicated Israel’s being sown and scattered throughout the lands of their captors. It will now signify that Hashem will sow her in the Land as a people belonging especially to Him. Just as one who sows a single kav of wheat may reap many kor, so Israel will multiply and flourish; converts will join them, and they will produce a holy crop for Hashem, for glory and splendor. This is as stated above: “The number of the Children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea.” In this way, the earth will answer the grain, causing the sowing to sprout and become “the branch of Hashem, for beauty and glory.” Regarding the daughter who was named Lo-Ruhamah, He says, I will have compassion upon Lo-Ruhamah: He will have compassion upon the exiled Ten Tribes. This corresponds to the heavens’ response, because compassion is of a lesser degree than kindness and signifies concealed miracles and Providence clothed in the natural order, which is associated with the heavens. Regarding the son whom He commanded to be called Lo-Ammi, representing the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, I will say to Lo-Ammi, “You are My people.” Corresponding to the earlier statement, “For you are not My people, and I will not be for you,” he will say, “My God.” For My Divine Presence will be revealed openly over the tribe of Judah. The miracles will no longer be clothed in the ways of nature but will occur through open Divine Providence. This corresponds to Hashem’s answering the heavens by pouring forth the bounty of His favor from His holy abode.
text.2_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem said to me again: After the first metaphor, in which He compared Israel to a married woman who commits harlotry against her husband and commanded the prophet likewise to marry a woman who was unfaithful to her husband, another command came to the prophet: Go, love a woman beloved by a companion yet committing adultery. He was to love a woman through a relationship of affection, not by taking her in marriage as he had done with the first woman. She was not to be a married woman committing harlotry against her husband, but an unmarried woman who had no husband through marriage. She had only a companion who loved her greatly, yet she committed adultery with other men as well in exchange for payment. Although she could not be called a harlot in the marital sense, since she had no husband, she nevertheless betrayed the companion who loved her. This serves as another metaphor for the congregation of Israel after its exile. At that time, Hashem sent them away from His presence, annulled the former betrothal, and Israel became like an unmarried woman. This occurred after He said, “You are not My people.” From then on, she is described as committing adultery rather than harlotry, because she has no permanent husband. Nevertheless, she is “beloved by a companion.” Although Hashem does not love her with the love of a husband, He loves her with the love of a companion. Although His love for her is not displayed publicly, He loves her and watches over her privately through concealed Providence, while they are unfaithful to Him. Thus He says, like Hashem’s love for the Children of Israel: The woman “beloved by a companion” represents Hashem’s love for the Children of Israel during their exile. He is not then their husband or betrothed, but loves them as a companion loves his concubine. Hosea was similarly commanded to take this woman as his companion, not as his wife. The woman’s adultery represents the fact that they turn toward other gods, turning away from Hashem, their companion, to practice idolatry. And they love raisin cakes: They are no longer in their former condition, in which the husband provided her sustenance while she went after her lovers because she imagined that they supplied it, as she said, “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water.” Now, in exile, she has no fixed source of sustenance—neither from her companion, who is not her husband, nor from her lovers, for she no longer has any true lovers. Instead, she resembles a degraded prostitute who commits harlotry merely for a cup of wine given to her by those who consort with her; they become her lovers through raisin cakes. Likewise, Israel in exile turns away from Hashem in exchange for something insignificant, as it says, “Because you did not serve Hashem your God joyfully amid an abundance of everything, you shall serve your enemies in hunger and thirst,” etc.
text.2_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: So I acquired her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver: He portrays himself as purchasing her from her companion and paying fifteen pieces of silver for her. This depicts two ideas. First, he did not acquire her as a wife, whose marriage payment is fifty pieces of silver, like the dowry of virgins. Rather, he acquired her as one purchases a female slave, whose price is thirty pieces of silver, as it says, “If the ox gores a male or female slave, he shall give their master thirty shekels of silver.” Likewise, the valuation of a woman between the ages of twenty and sixty is thirty shekels, as explained in the section concerning valuations. Second, he did not even pay the full thirty shekels for her, but only half—fifteen shekels. This represents the fact that she was not exclusively his, since she committed adultery, and therefore he paid only half her value. He treated her sustenance in the same manner, giving her a homer of barley and a lethekh of barley. A homer consists of thirty se’ah, while a lethekh consists of fifteen se’ah. Since she was not his wife, whom he would be obligated to provide generously with bread and water according to her dignity, but only resembled a poor woman whom he supported not from obligation but from compassion, he followed the rule that a poor traveler must be given no less than a loaf costing one pundion when four se’ah of wheat are sold for a sela. A sela is four dinars, so one se’ah costs one dinar; a dinar is six ma’ah, and a ma’ah is two pundion. Thus, one-twelfth of a se’ah is provided for a single meal. Accordingly, the homer, consisting of thirty se’ah, is sufficient for the daytime meals of the 360 days of the year. Yet instead of wheat bread, he gave her inferior barley bread, indicating her degraded state, in which she ate the food of animals. For her evening meal, he allotted only half the amount of her daytime meal, showing that he was not obligated to support her and therefore gave her only half, since at night she would go out to commit adultery with her paramours and deserved only half a portion. Even this consisted only of inferior barley.
text.2_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And I said to her, “You shall remain for me for many days”: He stipulated that she must wait for him for many days. Throughout that period, you shall not commit harlotry outside of marriage, nor shall you belong to another man through marriage; and I also will remain faithful to you, for after many days I will take you as my wife. In the allegory, Hashem acquired her during her exile for fifteen pieces of silver. During the period of exile, the Divine Name is incomplete, and only half of the Name is used—the letters yod and heh, whose numerical value is fifteen. Her provisions are allotted for only one year at a time, on each Rosh Hashanah, as our Sages explained concerning the verse “You shall be in terror night and day”: this refers to one who purchases enough wheat for only a single year. Moreover, her food is inferior barley. He commanded her to wait for Him for many days, until He extends His hand a second time to acquire the remnant of His people. He commanded her not to stray after idolatry and not to belong to another man by adopting a different faith from another master. He promised her that He too would remain faithful to her and wait to redeem her and betroth her to Himself forever in the future.
text.2_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: For many days: He explains the allegory: For many days the Children of Israel shall dwell in exile, waiting and hoping for Me to return to them as in former days. Without a king: They will have no king from the Davidic dynasty, whose kings sat upon the throne of Hashem and stood under His Providence. And without a prince: Yet neither will they place themselves under the celestial rulers, for they will wait for Hashem, as indicated by the commands, “You shall not commit harlotry, nor shall you belong to another man.” Without a sacrifice: During this period, they will not offer sacrifices to draw down Hashem’s bounty upon themselves, because the Temple and its service will have ceased. And without a pillar: Nevertheless, they will not erect sacred pillars for the Baals. And without an ephod: They will have no priest wearing an ephod through which he can learn the future. Nevertheless, they will be without teraphim: They will not consult teraphim in order to learn the future through them. Our Sages said: “In the days of Rehoboam, Israel rejected three things: the kingdom of the House of David, the Kingdom of Heaven, and the Temple.” Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya said: “Israel will not see signs of deliverance and redemption until they return and seek all three,” as it is written: “Afterward the Children of Israel shall return and seek Hashem their God”—this is the Kingdom of Heaven; “and David their king”—as literally stated; “and they shall come trembling to Hashem and to His goodness”—this is the Temple, as it is written, “this good mountain and the Lebanon.” Accordingly, He says that for many days they will remain without a king from the House of David, without sacrifices in the Temple, and without an ephod to reveal the future through the Divine Spirit, since the ephod spoke through the Divine Spirit, which came from the Kingdom of Heaven. Correspondingly, they will also have no prince, sacred pillar, or teraphim, which are the opposing counterparts of those three.
text.2_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Afterward the Children of Israel shall return and seek Hashem their God: This refers to the Kingdom of Heaven. And David their king: This refers to the kingdom of the House of David. And they shall come trembling to Hashem and to His goodness: They will then tremble in anticipation that He will restore His goodness and His Divine Presence in Zion, meaning the Temple, where He will dwell among them. This will occur last, as is explained everywhere. Likewise, the prescribed order was first to appoint a king, then to destroy the offspring of Amalek, and afterward to build the Temple, as our Sages taught (Sanhedrin 20b). The appointment of a king constitutes the crown of kingship. The destruction of Amalek will cause the Divine Name to become complete, with the House of David seated upon Hashem’s throne, exercising the Kingdom of Heaven upon earth. The crown of Torah will then be completed, for there will be a king and revelation of the future through the Divine Spirit, which operates through the power of the Divine Name. Afterward will come the building of the chosen Temple, with its sacrifices and the crown of priesthood. This will take place at the End of Days.
text.3_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: For Hashem has a grievance: The meaning of the verses is: “For Hashem has a grievance against the inhabitants of the land; nevertheless, let no man contend.” The prophet relates the people’s response. They say to the prophets and those who rebuke them: “Why do you contend with us and rebuke us? This grievance is Hashem’s grievance, for it is He who has a grievance against the inhabitants of the land because they have sinned against Him. Why should any man take up Hashem’s grievance? Let Hashem Himself prosecute His grievance and pour out His wrath upon everyone, but let no man involve himself in the dispute or offer rebuke.” They say: “Hashem indeed has a grievance against the inhabitants of the land, because there is neither truth, nor kindness, nor knowledge of God in the land.” That is, the commandments are divided into those governing relations between one person and another, whose foundation is that people practice truth and kindness toward one another—yet these are absent from the land—and those governing relations between a person and God, whose foundation is the knowledge of God, that they should know Hashem and His ways—yet this too is absent from the land. Instead, the opposite is found:
text.3_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Swearing and lying: They swear falsely in Hashem’s name and deny the existence of Hashem and His Providence. This is the opposite of the knowledge of God. Murdering, stealing, and committing adultery: These are the opposite of truth and kindness. Corresponding to the first five of the Ten Commandments, most of which govern the relationship between a person and God, he mentions swearing and denial. Swearing falsely violates “You shall not take Hashem’s name in vain,” while denial opposes “I am Hashem your God” and “You shall have no other gods,” as well as the commandment of the Sabbath, which establish belief in Hashem’s existence, His unity, and His individual Providence. Murder, theft, and adultery oppose the second five commandments. They have broken all bounds: That is, these transgressions have spread so extensively that bloodshed touches bloodshed because of the abundance of murder. This is the grievance Hashem has against the inhabitants of the land. Nevertheless, no person should involve himself in this grievance by contending with them or rebuking them on Hashem’s behalf. Rather:
text.3_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore the land shall mourn, etc.; yet let no man contend: Let Hashem prosecute His own grievance and destroy the land, until the land mourns and its inhabitants perish, and even the animals that cannot speak are destroyed; even the fish of the sea shall be gathered away. Hashem may do all this in prosecuting His grievance, provided only that no man contend on Hashem’s behalf and no man rebuke the people. All this constitutes the people’s response to the prophets. That is, they would rather have the land destroyed than listen to the prophets’ rebuke. And your people: He says to the Children of Israel, your people are like those who contend with a priest. That is, not only do they refuse to hear rebuke; on the contrary, they resemble people who quarrel with the priest who teaches knowledge. They say to the priest:
text.3_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall stumble by day: “You, the priest who teaches the people, have yourself stumbled upon corrupt paths in broad daylight, openly before the eyes of the sun.”
text.3_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And the prophet shall also stumble: The prophet who is with you and rebukes the people commits transgressions at night, in secret. “Thus, since you—the priest and the prophet who instruct and rebuke us—have yourselves stumbled into wrongdoing, your mother resembles you. I am like you—I, your mother, the nation and the congregation of Israel, am your mother, for individual people are the children of the nation. I have become like you and learned from you to act according to your deeds and abominations.” With these words they contend with the priest.
text.3_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: My people have become like you: This is Hashem’s statement to the priest. “My people have become like you through lack of knowledge; they lack knowledge just as you do, because you have rejected knowledge. In this respect, they have come to resemble you by rejecting knowledge as well, for they learned this from you. Therefore, I will reject you from serving as My priest, for ‘the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge, and people should seek Torah from his mouth.’ This is the priest’s essential function. Since you have rejected knowledge, you are no longer fit for the priesthood. More than this, you have forgotten the Torah of your God: You have entirely forgotten the Torah that you once knew. Therefore, I too will forget your children. At first, when you still remembered the Torah, although you had forgotten the knowledge of God, I nevertheless did not forget you, for I still hoped that your children would follow My Torah. As our Sages said, ‘If only they had abandoned Me but preserved My Torah, for by occupying themselves with it, the light within it would have restored them to the proper path.’ But now that you have forgotten the Torah as well, I too will forget your children, for there is no longer any hope that a righteous branch will sprout from them.
text.3_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: As they increased: As your children multiply and grow numerous, so they sinned against Me—so too will they continue to increase their sins—until I exchange their honor for disgrace. The honor of the priesthood consists in Hashem’s gift of the sacred offerings to them, permitting them to eat portions of the sacrifices from Hashem’s table. They resemble nobles who occupy the foremost positions in the kingdom and continually dine at the king’s table; the priests eat, and the owners of the sacrifices obtain atonement. But this honor of theirs will be exchanged for disgrace, for:
text.3_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: They feed upon the sin of My people: They do not eat from Hashem’s offerings in order “to bring transgression to an end and eliminate sin.” Rather, they feed upon the sin of My people. This is true, first, because the sinner does not obtain atonement through their service, which is not acceptable before Him; and second, because the priests themselves entice the people to sin so that they will bring sacrifices and provide the priests with something to eat. Not only do they cause the people to sin unintentionally, but they set their desire upon the people’s iniquity: They induce the people to commit deliberate transgressions by teaching them to imitate the priests’ own deliberate wrongdoing. He now explains:
text.3_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be, like people, like priest: The people will commit deliberate transgressions because they will become like the priest, learning to imitate him and perform his wicked deeds. Therefore, I will visit his ways upon him: I will punish the priest for his evil ways, and I will repay him for his deeds, measure for measure.
text.3_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: They shall eat but not be satisfied: When the priests were righteous, a blessing rested within them, and they were satisfied by the small amount they ate from Hashem’s offerings, as our Sages taught. Now, however, because “they feed upon the sin of My people,” they shall eat without being satisfied. Moreover, because they led the people into harlotry and encouraged them to pursue it, they shall not increase and shall not multiply sons and daughters. For they have abandoned Hashem, to preserve harlotry, wine, and new wine, which take away the heart. The priest was commanded to preserve Hashem’s charge and remain holy to his God: both by separating himself from harlotry, as it says, “They shall not take a harlot or a profaned woman,” and by abstaining from wine and intoxicating drink, as it says, “Do not drink wine or intoxicating drink when you enter the Tent of Meeting.” For harlotry and wine take possession of the heart and turn it away from the path of Torah and holiness. Yet they abandoned the preservation of Hashem’s charge and instead devoted themselves to preserving harlotry and wine, making these their charge in place of Hashem’s charge—even though this very charge takes away their hearts and leads them astray.
text.3_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: My people inquire of their wood: My people consult a wooden idol in order to obtain an answer from it, but it gives them no answer. Instead, another piece of wood gives them the reply: their staff—the rod prepared to strike them—will declare it to them. It will reveal to them that a spirit of harlotry has led them astray from the proper path, and that through this spirit they have strayed in harlotry from beneath their God. The metaphor means that through the rod that strikes them, it will become known to them that they have wandered from the proper path.
text.3_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: They sacrifice upon the mountaintops: There they strayed in harlotry from beneath their God. He depicts the sacrifices to idols—which constituted the principal form of worship and were performed communally before a great multitude—as taking place upon the mountaintops. And they burn incense: Incense was not a principal form of worship, and each individual performed it privately; therefore, they did this upon the hills beneath the mountains, each person alone, under oak and poplar. Moreover, their sacrifices and incense were accompanied by sexual immorality, for such conduct was connected with idolatry, as is well known. There were likewise two kinds of harlotry: public harlotry upon the mountains and secret harlotry upon the hills, as will be explained in the following verse.
text.3_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: Therefore your daughters shall commit harlotry: They will act as their fathers did, as he will explain. It was customary for daughters to go outside to meet their husbands, whereas daughters-in-law remained within the home (as stated in Judges, chapter 12). Therefore, the daughters shall commit harlotry, for harlotry denotes a woman’s straying from beneath her husband, and they were regarded as harlots. And your daughters-in-law shall commit adultery: Since the daughters-in-law remained at home, while the people had publicly permitted harlotry and forbidden sexual relations, their behavior was not regarded by them as harlotry but merely as adultery, a term that also includes the sexual misconduct of an unmarried woman.
text.3_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: No: I will not punish your daughters when they commit harlotry, because the sin does not originate with the daughters but with their fathers, from whom they learned to behave this way. For they withdraw with harlots and sacrifice with cult prostitutes. They sacrifice together with the cult prostitutes—women designated for sexual immorality who practiced it publicly. For the sacrifices were offered publicly before great gatherings, as stated, “They sacrifice upon the mountaintops,” and the men committed immorality with the cult prostitutes, who were themselves designated for idolatrous worship. As is well known, idolaters maintained cult prostitutes whose sexual relations they regarded as sacred and whose earnings were placed in the idol’s treasury. With the harlots, however—married women who secretly betrayed their husbands—the men withdrew from the gathering upon the mountaintops in order to commit immorality with them privately upon the hills, in concealed places. All this explains the statement, “His staff will declare to him that a spirit of harlotry has led them astray”: their desire for sexual immorality led them away from Hashem to practice idolatry, and the staff that strikes them will make this known to them. Therefore, he concludes, a people that does not understand shall be struck down. They will be beaten with a rod of punishment, yet they will not understand that they must return to the One who strikes them, and they will stumble and become exhausted from the abundance of blows.
text.3_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Though you commit harlotry: It was explained above (chapter 1, verse 1) that when Hosea began to prophesy in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, the kingdom of Judah was under the authority of the kingdom of Israel. This continued until the twenty-fourth year of Uzziah, when he began to reign independently. Judah was subordinate to the kingdom of Ephraim, and its people traveled to the cities of Israel, while they themselves still served Hashem during those days. The prophet therefore warns Judah not to enter the cities of Israel, where the calves and foreign worship were found, lest they learn from Israel’s conduct. Thus he says, Though you, Israel, commit harlotry: Since you, Israel—that is, the kingdom of Ephraim—have strayed in harlotry from your God, care must be taken that Judah not become guilty by learning from your deeds. He therefore commands the tribe of Judah: Do not enter Gilgal, and do not ascend to Beth-Aven, meaning Bethel, for the people practiced the worship of the calves in both places. As it says, “Come to Bethel and transgress; at Gilgal multiply transgression” (Amos 4:4), and “At Gilgal they sacrificed bulls” (below, Hosea 12:12). Both places bordered the territory of Judah, and the people of Judah would travel there. He therefore commands them to guard themselves from entering these places, for then you must not swear, ‘As Hashem lives.’ In Gilgal and Bethel, the people swear by the guilt-idol of Samaria and remain silent rather than mention Hashem’s name, whereas you, Judah, swear, “As Hashem lives.” Therefore, do not go there.
text.3_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: For: The meaning of the verse is: For now, when Hashem pastures them like a lamb in a broad meadow, Israel has rebelled like a stubborn heifer. In the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, Hashem had compassion upon Israel after the king of Aram had devastated them and made them like dust to be trampled. He delivered them through Jeroboam son of Joash, who restored Israel’s border from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah (II Kings 14:25). At that time, Hashem pastured them in a broad meadow—that is, He enlarged the borders of their land. He expected them to resemble a lamb that follows its shepherd and does not separate from the flock to wander upon wayward mountains. He thought that through this kindness they would follow Him and not rebel against Him. Instead, they rebelled like a stubborn heifer that, when led into a broad meadow, abandons its shepherd, turns away, and distances itself from him. Likewise, Israel then distanced itself from Hashem, who had pastured them and enlarged their borders. He now explains how they distanced themselves from Him:
text.3_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Ephraim is joined to idols: Their king—for the kingdom is called by the name Ephraim—is attached to idols and refuses to separate from their company, as it says of Jeroboam son of Joash, “He did what was evil in the eyes of Hashem; he did not depart from the sin of Jeroboam” (II Kings 14). Therefore, I command you, Judah: Leave him alone. Separate yourself from him; do not enter Gilgal and do not associate with him.
text.3_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Has departed: The meaning of the verse is: O her defenders! Their drinking has departed from its proper bounds; they have persistently led others into harlotry. He tells Judah, Leave him alone, and do not rely upon Ephraim’s defenders—its officers and warriors—who protected Judah at that time, when Judah was subordinate and weak. For the defenders of the kingdom of Ephraim possess three defects. First is drunkenness: their drinking has departed from its normal bounds. Second is harlotry and idolatry: not only do they themselves stray, but they persistently lead others into harlotry, enticing them toward sexual immorality and idolatry. Third, they love disgrace: they themselves love shameful, base, and contemptible things, and devote their affection to clinging to them.
text.3_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: The wind has bound him up: This wind—the spirit of drunkenness, the spirit of harlotry, and the evil and contemptuous spirit—has bound this bird in its wings and carries it aloft, causing it to fly away from its land to Assyria and Egypt, as it says below (Hosea 7:12), “I will bring them down like the birds of the heavens.” Consequently, they shall be ashamed because of their sacrifices that they offered to the calves.
text.4_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear this, O priests: These were the priests of the calves, who enticed the people not to go to Jerusalem, while the house of Israel allowed itself to be misled by them. And listen, O house of the king: They stationed guards along the roads and killed anyone who wished to make the pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Therefore, He says, for the judgment is against you, because Hashem’s judgment will come on your account, since you are the cause of all the evil.
text.4_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: For you were a snare at Mizpah: Mizpah and Tabor were two mountains along the route to Jerusalem. They stationed guards there to ensure that no one went up for the pilgrimage. He figuratively says that at Mizpah there was a snare to capture those passing through, while upon Tabor, which was a more spacious place, they spread a net all around the mountain to catch anyone ascending there. You, the house of the king, were the snare and the net, for all this was done at your command.
text.4_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And they have deeply pursued the slaughter of those who turn aside: Some people took care not to cross the mountains but turned aside from the road and descended deep into the valley, where the guards were not stationed. If they were caught along the way, the guards slaughtered them there. You, the house of the king, were the slaughter—that is, you were the ones who issued the orders to slaughter and murder them. The meaning of the following verses is: I am a rebuker of them all; I know that their deeds will not permit them to return to Hashem. The prophet says: “I am the prophet who serves as a rebuker of them all, having been appointed to admonish all the groups mentioned above with words of correction and restore them through repentance. Yet I know that at present my rebuke will accomplish nothing, because:”
text.4_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: I know Ephraim: And Israel is not hidden from Me. I know their nature and disposition well. For now the rebuke I address to them will be of no avail, for now you, Ephraim, have led others into harlotry. That is, Ephraim—the royal house—entices the people to stray after the calves, and as a result, Israel has become defiled, for the people have been defiled through Ephraim’s influence. Therefore, I know that at present:
text.4_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Their deeds will not permit them to return to Hashem their God: At present, they will not abandon their evil deeds in order to return to Hashem, and my rebuke will not succeed in bringing them to repentance. This is for two reasons. First, a spirit of harlotry is within them: They are filled with a spirit of heresy and with desire for idolatry and sexual immorality. Second, they do not know Hashem. Therefore, I know that at this time they will not relinquish or abandon their evil deeds, and the correction with which I admonish them will be of no avail. Nevertheless, although my rebuke will not help them now, a time will come when they will take this correction to heart. This will occur when:
text.4_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And the pride of Israel shall testify against him: When his pride is humbled and he recognizes within himself that he is being punished for his deeds; when Israel and Ephraim stumble and fall and recognize that this has occurred because of their iniquity; and Judah also stumbles with them and receives his punishment—then, at that time, they will accept correction, for then:
text.4_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: With their flocks and their cattle they shall go to seek Hashem: They will no longer station guards to prevent the people from going to Jerusalem. On the contrary, they will then go to seek Hashem in Jerusalem, bringing sheep and cattle with them to offer in the Temple. But at that point their search will not help them, for they will no longer find Him, since He has already withdrawn from them and distanced Himself from them. This also means that by seeking Hashem externally through sacrifices, they will not find Him. For Hashem is not found merely within His Temple, but within the heart of the nation and the depths of their souls. There is His dwelling when they sanctify themselves and follow His commandments, as it says, “I will dwell within them.” Since He has withdrawn from them and from within them, they will not find Him outside themselves.
text.4_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: They have betrayed Hashem: Here he relates how the dynasty of Jehu came to an end, as stated (in chapter 1): “In a little while, I will visit the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu.” This occurred when Zechariah son of Jeroboam became king. He reigned for six months, until Shallum son of Jabesh conspired against him, struck him before the people, and reigned in Samaria for one month (as stated in II Kings 15). Therefore, he says, They have betrayed Hashem, for they have begotten alien children: This refers to Zechariah, whose conduct made him alien to the Omnipresent. Therefore, now a month shall devour them: This refers to Shallum son of Jabesh, who reigned for one month. He devoured and destroyed their portions—that is, within a single month he consumed the entire house of Jehu.
text.4_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Sound the shofar: It was explained above (chapter 1, verse 1, and chapter 4, verse 15) that when Jeroboam son of Joash reigned, at which time Hosea began to prophesy, the tribes of Judah and Benjamin were subordinate to the kingdom of Ephraim. This had been the case since Joash conquered Amaziah, king of Judah. Likewise, in the days of Pekah son of Remaliah, the Children of Israel fought against the people of Judah and brought them under their control. This occurred during the reign of Ahaz (as related in II Kings and Isaiah, chapter 7). The territory of Benjamin bordered that of the descendants of Joseph, as stated in Joshua, and during these periods it was under the kingdom of Ephraim. The prophet commands the people of Benjamin to sound the shofar in Gibeah, which belonged to Benjamin, and the trumpet in Ramah, which also belonged to Benjamin, and to sound an alarm in Beth-Aven, which likewise fell within Benjamin’s allotted territory, as it says in Joshua concerning Benjamin’s territory, “and its boundary extended toward the wilderness of Beth-Aven.” In all these places, they are to sound the alarm and warn the people, saying, “After you, Benjamin!”—that they should not follow the kingdom of Ephraim but should follow you, Benjamin, who is joined to the kingdom of Judah, and separate themselves from the kingdom of Ephraim.
