text.4_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Ephraim: He explains why they should separate themselves from the kingdom of Ephraim: because Ephraim shall become desolate on the day of punishment—the day appointed by Hashem to chastise them for their sins and repay them for their deeds. The phrase among the tribes of Israel belongs with what follows. The meaning and order of the verse are:
text.4_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Among the tribes of Israel, the princes of Judah were like those who move a boundary; I have made known with certainty that I will pour out My wrath upon them like water. That is, among the tribes of Israel—the Ten Tribes—were those who had now become the princes of Judah, meaning that they had become rulers exercising authority over Judah. In this respect, they resembled those who move a boundary, for they encroached upon the territory of the kingdom of the House of David. Judah properly belongs to the Davidic kingdom, since Hashem promised David that He would always leave a lamp for his descendants by preserving one tribe for him, as stated in I Kings 11. Concerning these tribes of Israel, I have made known with certainty—through a firm and irrevocable decree—that I will pour out My wrath upon them like water, as stated in Isaiah 7: “Within another sixty-five years, Ephraim shall be shattered as a people.” The defining character of overflowing wrath is that, in His fury, He punishes the one who did not sin together with the sinner. The principal sinner was the tribe of Ephraim—the royal house—which established the calves. The other tribes of Israel, the people who followed them, were enticed and could be considered as having acted under pressure or deception. Nevertheless, because of Hashem’s burning anger against Ephraim, the general wrath will overflow and punish the other tribes as well, like water that is poured out and spreads in every direction.
text.4_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Ephraim is oppressed: The other tribes will become plunder only because of the general overflow of Divine wrath, not as a result of strict judgment. The tribe of Ephraim itself, however, which caused the multitude to sin, will be crushed by judgment—not merely because of overflowing wrath, but according to justice and law. For he willingly—that is, he was the first to initiate the transgression—followed the command of Jeroboam, who came from his own tribe, and they supported him in establishing the calves and leading the multitude into sin.
text.4_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And I am like a moth to Ephraim: That which consumes and destroys Ephraim and Judah is not a natural force but an act of Divine Providence, for it is I who destroy them like a moth and like decay, which consume and cause everything to disintegrate. He compares Hashem to a moth to Ephraim and decay to the house of Judah. A moth enters an object from outside, whereas decay arises from within the object itself as it rots and disintegrates. Accordingly, he depicts Hashem as coming to Ephraim from outside to destroy it, for He does not dwell in Ephraim; His Divine Presence dwells in Zion, and from Zion He comes to consume and destroy Ephraim like a moth entering from outside. In Judah, however, where He dwells, He resembles decay, whose cause is present within the object itself.
text.4_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And Ephraim saw his sickness: But they did not understand that it was Hashem who was striking and destroying them. They imagined that it was a natural sickness and wound, for which natural remedies must be sought to remove the illness and restore the body’s health. Ephraim therefore appealed to the king of Assyria, expecting him to cure the sickness of the body politic through his army and forces. This refers to Menahem son of Gadi sending a thousand talents of silver to Pul, king of Assyria, so that he would strengthen the kingdom in Menahem’s hands (as stated in II Kings 15:19). Ahaz likewise sent the king of Assyria a bribe and tribute so that he would support him against Pekah son of Remaliah and Rezin king of Aram, who were waging war against him, as related (there, chapter 16). He depicts Ephraim as seeing his sickness and Judah as seeing his wound, for there is a distinction between sickness and a wound. Sickness arises internally because the body’s constitution has become corrupted or weakened, whereas a wound results from an external blow and is treated by applying medicinal powders externally. Ephraim appealed to the king of Assyria to secure the kingdom against the rebellion that had arisen from within, resembling an internal sickness. Judah appealed to him to save it from the kings who attacked and struck it from outside, resembling a wound inflicted externally. And Ephraim went to Assyria so that it would suppress the internal rebellion and cure the sickness. And he sent: Judah sent to the contentious king—that is, it sent messengers to the king of Assyria so that he would contend on Judah’s behalf against Pekah and Rezin, who had risen against it. This was the external wound. Neither kingdom obtained what it hoped for. Regarding Ephraim’s appeal to cure its internal sickness, He says, but he cannot heal you, as it says concerning Menahem son of Gadi, “He did not remain there in the land.” Regarding Judah’s appeal that he heal its external wound, He says, nor can he remove the wound from you, as it says concerning Ahaz (II Chronicles 28), “He distressed him and did not strengthen him.”
text.4_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: For I am like a lion to Ephraim: This is not a natural sickness or wound that anyone can heal or from which anyone can rescue them, for it is I who strike them, like a mature lion and a young lion. Naturalists have stated that while a lion is still young, when it is called a kefir, it does not leave its lair to seize prey. Instead, it remains there in ambush and preys only upon whatever approaches its dwelling. But when it reaches the stage of the mature lion, called a shachal, it goes outside to hunt and bring prey back to its lionesses. Therefore, He says, For I am like a mature lion to Ephraim and like a young lion to the house of Judah. Toward Ephraim, Hashem resembles a mature lion that comes from elsewhere to seize its prey; likewise, Hashem comes against them from Zion, where His shelter and dwelling are found. Toward the house of Judah, however, He resembles a young lion that seizes prey in the very place where it dwells, for His dwelling is within Judah. This is the same idea expressed above: “For I am like a moth to Ephraim and like decay to the house of Judah.”
text.4_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: I, even I: However it occurs, their adversity is neither natural nor accidental, but comes through Divine Providence, for I, even I, am the One who seizes the prey. In Ephraim, I will tear and depart—I will carry the prey away with Me to My own place, like the mature lion that seizes its prey and carries it far away. In Judah, however, where I seize the prey within My own lair, I will carry it off but will not depart, because My dwelling is there, like the young lion. In both forms of seizure, there is no one who can rescue from My hand, and Assyria will be unable to help you.
text.4_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: I will depart: In reference to the statement, “I will tear and depart,” He adds that not only will I depart from Ephraim for Jerusalem, but I will also return to My place—I will withdraw from Zion as well and return to heaven, distancing Myself from them entirely—until they acknowledge their guilt. This will continue until they return in repentance on their own, by acknowledging their guilt and seeking My face—that is, recognizing their wrongdoing, seeking My presence, and repenting. Alternatively, if they do not recognize their guilt on their own, then at least in their distress they will seek Me early: many evils and afflictions will befall them, and the severity of their troubles will then cause them to seek Me.
text.5_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Come, let us return: After saying that in their distress they will seek Hashem’s presence, the prophet now expresses what they will say when they seek Hashem and how Hashem will answer them. They will say to one another, Come, let us return to Hashem, for He has torn us. Our afflictions did not arise naturally but came from Him; therefore, He alone can heal us. Regarding the internal sickness that requires healing, they will say, He is the One who tore us, and He will heal us. Regarding the external wound that requires binding, they will say, He struck us, and He will bind our wounds. For deliverance depends upon Him alone, as stated above, “He cannot heal you,” etc.
text.5_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: He will revive us after two days: The Ten Tribes were exiled by Sennacherib in three stages, as it says, “As in the former time He dealt lightly,” etc., “but in the latter time He dealt more severely” (Isaiah 8:23). Likewise, the tribe of Judah was exiled three times by Nebuchadnezzar, as explained in II Kings and Jeremiah. They therefore ask that He restore them to life after the first two days, which were days of punishment. And on the third day—the third exile, when they fell completely—He will raise us up from our downfall, and we shall live before Him and serve Hashem.
text.5_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And let us know: Then let us pursue the knowledge of Hashem. That is, we will strive to grasp the truths concerning Hashem’s Providence and to understand the ways of His Providence, goodness, and kindness, until our knowledge of Him becomes as clear as the dawn, whose emergence is certain. It also means that the more we strive to know Him, the more fully our knowledge of Him will be revealed, as it says, “The path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, growing ever brighter until the day is firmly established.” He therefore compares it to the dawn, whose light appears gradually until the sun rises. Likewise, the light of our knowledge of Him and of His salvation will shine upon us. And He will come to us like rain: Rain comes through the earth’s preparation, for moist vapors rise from the earth into the atmosphere, and “when the clouds are filled with rain, they pour it upon the earth.” Likewise, through our actions and an awakening from below, He will again shower upon us rains of generosity—the rains of understanding and salvation. Even if He does not come immediately like rain arriving in its proper season, He will nevertheless come at the End of Days like the latter rain that waters the earth, causing it to bring forth and sprout.
text.5_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: What shall I do? This is Hashem’s response: You, Ephraim, and likewise you, Judah—what shall I do with you? For your kindness is like a morning cloud. The principal thing Hashem requires of you is to practice justice and love kindness, the essential requirement being that one act kindly toward other people. Kindness also includes the commandments between a person and God that are performed out of piety, which are called “a Torah of kindness,” as I have explained elsewhere. Yet your kindness resembles a morning cloud, which rises and disperses when the sun shines and sends no saturating rain upon the earth. How, then, can you ask that He come to you like rain? There can be no rain without clouds, and no rain will develop from a morning cloud. Even when you resemble dew, which forms at night from the droplets rising from the plants and persists throughout the night, nevertheless, it vanishes early. As soon as the sun rises, there is neither dew nor rain upon you. Likewise, as soon as you rise to pursue your own desires and ways, the thread of kindness is broken, and there is neither kindness nor knowledge of God in the land.
text.5_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore: The meaning of the verses is: Therefore I engraved My words upon the prophets, whom I caused to be killed through the words of My mouth, for I desire kindness and not sacrifice. The statement, “And your judgments go forth like light,” is parenthetical. He presents a sublime metaphor. Hashem sent His prophets to rebuke the people, who imagined that by continually offering abundant sacrifices and burnt offerings they could give Hashem a bribe or gift, appease Him, and obtain atonement, while remaining free to commit every evil. As it says, “Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, and swear falsely, and then come and stand before Me in this house upon which My name is called and say, ‘We are saved’?” The prophets conveyed to them the words of Hashem’s mouth—that Hashem says, For I desire kindness and not sacrifice: He does not desire sacrifices and burnt offerings, but that they practice kindness and possess knowledge of God. The people rose against the prophets and killed them because of this prophecy. Scripture therefore depicts Hashem as having killed the prophets through the words of His mouth: they were killed because they proclaimed the words of His mouth as His messengers, so Hashem was indirectly the cause of their deaths, as though He Himself had killed them. Yet because the prophets were killed for this declaration and sacrificed their lives to proclaim, For I desire kindness and not sacrifice, these words remained permanently engraved in the hearts of later generations, like an inscription carved with an iron pen upon tablets of rock and stone as an eternal memorial. The prophet thus depicts the bodies of the slain prophets as monuments of rock and tablets of stone upon which Hashem engraved the words, For I desire kindness and not sacrifice. Thus He says, Therefore—because your kindness resembles a morning cloud, and you neither practice kindness nor know God—I engraved My words upon the prophets: Upon the bodies of the prophets, whom I caused to be killed through the words of My mouth, I carved and inscribed with an iron pen the declaration, For I desire kindness and not sacrifice. The original purpose of the peace offerings and other sacrifices that you bring was that their meat should be given to the poor to eat in holiness. My principal desire is therefore the kindness, not the sacrifice.
text.5_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And I desire knowledge of God more than burnt offerings: The essential purpose of the burnt offering, which is consumed entirely for the Most High, is that a person should know Hashem and recognize that he ought to offer himself entirely upon His altar as an acceptable offering. Thus, Hashem’s principal desire is the knowledge of God, not the burnt offering. This message likewise remained engraved and carved into the bodies of the slain prophets. The statement, and your judgments go forth like light, is parenthetical. It is as though He says: “If your sword devours your prophets like a destroying lion, how can your judgment emerge into the light, and how can you be vindicated in your case?”
text.5_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: But they: The seer now relates how the prophets were killed in those days, portraying it through an exceptionally elevated and sublime metaphor. Hashem’s prophets were killed by the kings of Israel on two occasions. First, we find in Kings that all Hashem’s prophets were killed in the days of Ahab by his wife Jezebel. All the prophets of that time were disciples of Elijah, as is evident from Scripture, and Elijah was one of the inhabitants of Gilead (as stated in I Kings 17). For this reason, our Sages held in the Midrash that Elijah descended from Benjamin, since the Benjaminites took wives from Jabesh-gilead (as stated in Judges 21:9–10) and settled there; Elijah was one of their descendants and remained a resident of Jabesh-gilead. From this we learn that the disciples of the prophets belonging to Elijah’s academy who were killed met their deaths in Gilead. Second, prophets were killed in Shechem during the days of Jeroboam. When Jeroboam became king and selected Shechem—which had been a Levitical city of refuge—as his royal city, prophets were undoubtedly present there who prophesied and rebuked him concerning the calves he had established, and he killed and destroyed them. The seer imaginatively compares the murder of Hashem’s prophets in Gilead and Shechem with killings that occurred in those same two places in ancient times because of zeal for Hashem against sexual immorality. In Gilead, during the episode of the concubine at Gibeah, the Children of Israel killed the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead because they had violated the covenant, oath, and ban Israel had imposed upon anyone who failed to join Hashem’s assembly in avenging the sexual outrage committed at Gibeah. At Shechem, the sons of Jacob likewise killed the men of Shechem because of the sexual outrage and disgrace committed against Jacob’s daughter. With his imagination now ranging back to those ancient times, when people were killed in Gilead and Shechem out of zeal for Hashem against sexual immorality, the seer speaks bitterly of the murder of Hashem’s prophets in those same places. He depicts the murderers as similarly displaying zeal—but now for the calves and Baal, which the prophets had denounced—as though they were avenging sexual immorality and the violation of a covenant and oath, as in ancient times. Thus he says, But they—the prophets—were regarded by them like those men who violated the covenant that the Children of Israel made during the episode of Gibeah, requiring everyone to join the army. The inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead violated that covenant, and there they betrayed Me. He explains: Gilead is a city of evildoers. Its inhabitants were the men who violated the covenant and oath and betrayed Hashem by failing to go up to Mizpah for the war against Gibeah. Consequently, it became tracked with blood, for they were all killed and their blood was shed. Now the prophets were likewise killed there in Gilead, as though they too had violated the covenant and betrayed Hashem.
text.5_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And as a man would expect: The murder of the prophets at Shechem was likewise portrayed as though the prophets had committed the sexual immorality for which the inhabitants of Shechem were killed in ancient times. Thus he says: As a man would wait and expect, if he saw bands of assembled priests traveling along the road to murder at Shechem—going toward Shechem to kill people there—he would certainly assume that these priests were going to commit murder because the people of Shechem had committed an outrage. He would suppose that the priests were displaying zeal against sexual immorality, just as Jacob’s sons had displayed zeal over the outrage committed at Shechem in ancient times. Likewise, when the priests of the calves went to kill Hashem’s prophets, they regarded their journey as though the prophets had committed sexual immorality and a disgraceful act in Israel. But it was not the prophets who had committed the outrage. On the contrary:
text.5_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: In the house of Israel I have seen a horrifying thing, for there is harlotry in Ephraim: Ephraim committed harlotry by straying after idolatry, and through them Israel became defiled. Because Ephraim, the ruling tribe, committed harlotry, the other tribes were defiled as well. The harlotry was found among them, not among the murdered prophets.
text.5_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Judah also: This refers back to what He said above: “What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah? For your kindness is like a morning cloud,” where He addressed Judah as well. He first explained Ephraim’s sin—the killing of the prophets—and now returns to Judah. He says: “Judah too, your kindness is like a morning cloud.” Yet He continues, He has appointed a harvest for you when I restore the captivity of My people. Your kindness will produce a harvest for you, in accordance with the verse, “Sow righteousness for yourselves; reap according to kindness.” You will reap the fruit of kindness when I restore the captivity of My people—that is, in the days of Hezekiah, when Hashem restored their fortunes and they were delivered through Him. At that time, kindness produced its harvest, as it says, “The surviving remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root below and produce fruit above” (Isaiah 37:31).
text.6_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: When I would heal Israel: This continues the preceding statement that Judah’s kindness will produce a harvest when Hashem restores their fortunes. In contrast, He says that this will not occur for Israel: their kindness will produce no harvest. For whenever I wish to heal Israel and restore their fortunes as well, the iniquity of Ephraim is exposed. Whereas their iniquity had previously been concealed, they then begin to act perversely openly and publicly. Thus, when Hashem bestowed goodness upon Israel in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash—when He restored Israel’s fortunes and its border from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah—they began to sin openly. The iniquity of Ephraim refers to their corruption in matters of faith between a person and God, while the evils of Samaria refer to the wrongs they committed against one another. Corresponding to “the iniquity of Ephraim is exposed,” he explains, for they have practiced falsehood by being false to their faith in Hashem and practicing idolatry. Corresponding to “the evils of Samaria are exposed,” he says, a thief enters, while a band raids outside. Formerly, only a single thief entered, and even he came secretly, like a thief stealing unseen. Now, however, an entire band carries out raids: no longer does a lone thief enter, nor do they come stealthily like thieves. Instead, a band raids outside openly, in broad daylight.
text.6_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: They do not say in their hearts: When adversity befell them, they thought in their hearts that I remembered their wickedness and was punishing them for it; therefore, their wrongdoing was not displayed so openly. But when I sought to heal them and enlarged their borders, they no longer said in their hearts that I remembered all their wickedness. They imagined that I had forgotten their wrongdoing and would not punish them, and therefore they committed sins publicly. Yet why should I need to remember their former wickedness? Now their own deeds surround them—the evil deeds they are presently committing encompass them—and they are before My face, standing before Me at this very moment. There is therefore no need to recall their earlier sins.
text.6_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: With their wickedness: From this point onward, the prophet begins to describe how they fell through the king of Assyria, who exiled them from their land. He first explains the cause that brought all this about. The initial cause was their rebellion against their kings and their murder of them. First, Shallum son of Jabesh conspired against Zechariah son of Jeroboam and struck him down before the people. Menahem son of Gadi then rose against Shallum, killed him, and reigned in his place. This caused Pul, king of Assyria, to invade the land, whereupon Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver to secure the kingdom in his own hands (II Kings 15:19). Afterward, Pekah son of Remaliah conspired against Pekahiah son of Menahem, killed him, and reigned in his place. Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, then invaded and exiled Zebulun and Naphtali; this came about through Ahaz (as related there in chapter 16). Afterward, Hoshea son of Elah struck Pekah and reigned in his place. Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, then came against him, and Hoshea became his vassal. The king of Assyria discovered a conspiracy by Hoshea, for he had sent messengers to So, king of Egypt. The king of Assyria seized him, imprisoned him, besieged Samaria, and exiled Israel to Assyria (there, chapter 17). It will become clear from the words of the book that the king of Assyria’s discovery of Hoshea’s conspiracy also resulted from denunciation by certain Israelites. They rebelled against Hoshea, devised schemes to destroy him, and revealed to the king of Assyria that Hoshea intended to rebel against him. Concerning these events, the seer delivered his prophecies from this point until the end of the book. With this introduction, we can proceed to the explanation. He says that while they were still loyal to their king, they gladdened the king with their wickedness, striving through their wicked deeds to please the king, and the princes with their falsehoods. This was before the rebellion. At that time:
text.6_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: They are all adulterers: They all occupied themselves with adultery, like an oven heated by a baker. In his metaphor, he compares the inclination toward sexual immorality to the flame that ignites, heats, and warms an oven, for likewise it kindles the fire of sexual desire. The baker who heats the oven sits throughout the night tending its fire. If he dozes off, another person awakens him from his sleep so that he will not allow the oven to cool. He can sleep only while kneading a fresh batch of dough and waiting for it to ferment until it is ready to be baked. At that point, from the kneading of the dough until it has fermented, the one who awakens him ceases and does not rouse him from sleep. Likewise, the faculty of desire gives a person no rest but continually awakens his passion. It subsides only for the brief interval after he has committed adultery, until his desire renews its strength. They behave this way while they are at peace with the king and the princes. But:
text.6_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: The day of our king: When the day of the king’s downfall arrived—the day of the rebellion when they intended to kill him—they did not occupy themselves with adultery during the preceding night. Instead, the conspirators assembled to deliberate on how to carry out the schemes of their hearts. While meeting together, they drank wine with the princes throughout the night, until the princes became sick from the wine. Consequently, the king’s officers were unable to remain vigilant against the conspiracy or protect the king’s life. Thus he says that they then made the princes sick through the heat of wine—that is, through the wine’s intoxicating warmth. The wine extended its hand among the scoffers: The power of the wine then prevailed, advancing among the scoffers with all its forces.
text.6_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: For they drew near: On that night, they brought their hearts—resembling an oven ready to be heated by flames—close to one another. That is, each revealed the hidden thoughts of his heart, and they shared their secrets with one another while lying in wait to kill the king, deliberating over how they would put him to death. Therefore, all night their baker slept: On that night they did not awaken the baker—the inclination toward lust and sexual immorality—but allowed it to sleep and rest. They did not occupy themselves with adultery, but with rebellion and murder. In the morning, however, it burned like a flaming fire: When morning came, the rebellion was completed and they killed the king. The oven—their hearts and inward parts—then burned, but not with the ordinary fire used to heat an oven for baking bread. It was ignited with a flaming fire, whose nature is to consume and devour everything that comes near it, even from a distance. That is, the active force then kindled within them was not the inclination of desire, but the aroused force of anger—jealousy, fury, and murderous rage—to kill, destroy, and annihilate. For then:
text.6_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: They all grew hot like an oven: At that point, no baker was needed to heat the oven, for they themselves were the oven, and they themselves were heated by the flame—the flame of rebellion, which resembled a consuming fire. And they devoured their judges: In this manner, all their kings fell, for they killed all their kings through conspiracy and rebellion. Thus Zechariah son of Jeroboam, Shallum son of Jabesh, Pekahiah son of Menahem, and Pekah son of Remaliah were killed; likewise, Hoshea was taken captive by the enemy because of the rebellion, as explained above. This caused their exile and destruction. It befell them because none among them called upon Me, for both they and their kings were wicked idolaters.
text.6_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Ephraim: Through their killing of their kings, it came about that Ephraim mingled and mixed among the nations. Menahem summoned the king of Assyria to assist him in securing the throne. When Pekah conspired against Pekahiah son of Menahem, the king of Assyria came to champion his cause; and while doing so, he also championed the cause of the king of Judah and exiled the land of Naphtali. Afterward, when Hoshea killed Pekah, the king of Assyria came against Hoshea, as explained above in verse 3. They brought all this upon themselves through the killing of their kings. Consequently, Ephraim became a cake that was not turned. Since he has thus far spoken through the metaphor of an oven, he now says figuratively that despite everything, they were not properly baked in the oven heated by the fire of their wrath. Instead, Ephraim resembled a cake baked upon coals, which must be turned several times so that it bakes on every side. If it is not turned, it has two defects: the coals burn the underside lying closest to them, while the upper side remains unbaked and unfit to be eaten. The allegorical meaning will be explained in the following verse.
text.6_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: They have devoured: He explains the allegory. Just as the underside of an unturned cake is consumed by the coals—representing an external force, namely the fire, consuming the cake’s substance—so strangers have devoured his strength, yet he does not know it. The king of Assyria consumed their strength, took their wealth, and exiled them. And just as the upper side of this cake remains unbaked, leaving its dough loose and soft, so too gray hairs have spread upon him, yet he does not know it. They resemble an aged man whose vitality and the marrow of his bones have been consumed by old age, leaving his constitution feeble and his limbs weak. Likewise, they themselves became weak, and their strength faded like that of an elderly man whose vigor has departed.
text.6_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And it testifies: In reference to what was stated above (5:5)—that when Israel’s pride would testify against him, “they would go with their flocks and cattle to seek Hashem” and return in repentance—he now says that although the pride of Israel testified against him, they nevertheless did not humble themselves before Hashem and did not return to Hashem in repentance. Nor did they seek Him despite all this through sacrifices and prayer; instead, they sought assistance from the nations.
text.6_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And Ephraim became like a foolish dove without sense: He acted entirely without judgment or understanding, for they called to Egypt, and then went to Assyria. Since they were subject to the kingdom of Assyria, they should not have called upon Egypt for assistance. This caused their exile, for the king of Assyria discovered that Hoshea was conspiring against him by sending messengers to So, king of Egypt. He therefore seized Hoshea, imprisoned him, besieged Samaria, and exiled Israel to Assyria. There was yet another act of foolishness: after appealing to Egypt, Hoshea went to Assyria. This is implied by the statement in II Kings 17:4: “The king of Assyria seized him and confined him in prison. Then the king of Assyria invaded the entire land, went up against Samaria, and besieged it for three years.” This implies that Hoshea went out to meet the king of Assyria as a submissive servant. There the king arrested him and prevented him from returning to Samaria, after which he invaded the land. Had Hoshea remained in Samaria, the king could not have seized him, since he required a three-year siege to capture the city. This was therefore an act of extraordinary foolishness: knowing that he had rebelled against the king of Assyria and had sent to Egypt, he should not have gone to Assyria and delivered himself into the king’s hands. Thus it says:
text.6_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: When they go: Hoshea’s going to Assyria came from Hashem, so that through it I would spread My net over them; I would bring them down like a bird of the heavens. In this respect, he resembled a bird flying in the heavens, which the hunter’s hand cannot reach at such a height. Instead, the hunter spreads a net for it, and the bird descends into the net and is caught there. Likewise, the king of Assyria could not have reached Hoshea while he remained within the fortified city of Samaria. But like a foolish dove, Hoshea was enticed to descend from his place into the net—that is, to go to the king of Assyria. There he was caught in the net and confined in prison. This occurred through Hashem’s Providence, which led him astray. I will chastise them: The meaning and order of the words is: When they listen, I will chastise them before their congregation, and I will redeem them. That is, even then they still had a means of deliverance, had they listened to My correction and rebuke. Thus He says, when they listen. I thought that if they would listen to correction, then I would chastise them before their congregation—I would address words of correction to them publicly—namely, I would tell them to observe that—…
text.6_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Woe to them, because they have wandered from Me: This is how I would chastise them through My correction, and thereby I would redeem them. Once they listened to this correction and returned to Me by taking to heart what sin causes, I would redeem them from the hand of the king of Assyria. But they spoke lies against Me: They did not allow this suffering to correct them, did not listen to rebuke, and did not take to heart that the calamity had befallen them because they had wandered from Hashem. Instead, they spoke lies against Hashem, denying His Providence and His punishment.
text.6_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: They did not cry out to Me from their hearts: Even when they wailed upon their beds because of their many afflictions, they merely lamented; they did not cry out to Hashem in prayer. Even when they did cry out to Him, it did not come from their hearts but only outwardly from their lips. For grain and wine they wander about: They travel from place to place in order to obtain grain and wine, while they rebel against Me—behaving toward Me like a stubborn and rebellious son who refuses to obey his father and is a glutton and drunkard.
text.6_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And I chastised them: When I chastised this stubborn and rebellious son, My intention was that through it I would strengthen their arms—that they would repent, whereupon I would strengthen their hands—as stated, “I will chastise them before their congregation, and I will redeem them.” But they devise evil against Me: They imagine that I am the source of evil and fail to understand that My intention is for their benefit.
text.6_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: They return, but not upward: They will escape from the net mentioned above—“I will spread My net over them; I will bring them down like a bird of the heavens.” Yet after this bird escapes from the net, it will not return upward to fly aloft, but will merely pass from one net into another. Likewise, they fled from the net of Egypt into the net of Assyria. Their princes were like a treacherous bow; they shall fall by the sword because of the fury of their tongues. The meaning is: Their princes were like a treacherous bow. This refers to the princes who went to the king of Assyria and informed against Hoshea son of Elah, telling him that Hoshea had rebelled and sent tribute to So, king of Egypt. They imagined that through this denunciation they were shooting the arrow of their bow at Hoshea. But the king of Assyria subsequently besieged Samaria and killed them as well. They therefore resembled a treacherous bow whose arrow recoils into the heart of the archer. Likewise, the arrows of their tongues returned against their own hearts. That is, their princes, who shot arrows through the fury of their tongues by slandering their king, would themselves fall by the sword of the king of Assyria. Thus, they resembled a treacherous bow. This was the cause of their derision in the land of Egypt: The Egyptians mocked them there for having become like a treacherous bow.
text.7_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Put the shofar to your palate: Hashem tells the prophet to place a shofar against his palate, hasten to fly like an eagle, and stand upon the house of Hashem, where he is to sound the shofar. For when a matter of great importance or a major announcement arose, they would sound the shofar at the house of Hashem. He commanded the prophet to stand high upon the Temple so that the sound of the shofar could be heard throughout the ends of the land. He was to sound it and proclaim that all the calamity had befallen them because they transgressed My covenant and rebelled against My Torah. He was also commanded to sound the shofar at the house of Hashem so that Judah too would hear and return to Hashem in the days of Hezekiah. For the king of Assyria came against them as well, and Hashem hastened like an eagle to rescue His nest, as it says, “Like hovering birds, so will Hashem protect Jerusalem” (Isaiah 31:5).
text.7_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: They shall cry out to Me: In contrast to what was stated above, “They did not cry out to Me from their hearts,” tell Israel to cry out to Me and say, “My God, we know You.” We recognize You and understand that this calamity has come from You through Divine Providence as punishment for our rebellion against You.
text.7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Israel has rejected: They will say all this in their outcry: We know that because Israel rejected what is good, therefore the enemy pursues him. This is not an accident but a punishment from Hashem.
text.7_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: They appointed kings, but not from Me: The kings they selected were appointed on their own initiative, not through a prophet acting by Hashem’s command. Afterward, they removed them from the kingship, but I did not acknowledge it, for this too was contrary to Hashem’s will. Apparently, two kings were removed from the throne because they did not uphold the worship of the calves. The first was Shallum son of Jabesh, of whom Scripture does not say, “He did what was evil in the eyes of Hashem,” as it says of every other king of Israel. Even concerning Zimri, who reigned for only seven days, it says, “He died for the sins he committed by following the way of Jeroboam.” All the more should this have been stated concerning Shallum, who reigned for an entire month. It is therefore evident that he did not follow Jeroboam’s way. One faction in Israel supported him in this, while an opposing faction wished to strengthen the worship of the calves. This latter faction supported Menahem son of Gadi, who rose against Shallum and killed him. Menahem therefore had to give Pul, king of Assyria, a thousand talents of silver to secure the kingdom in his hands, because Shallum’s supporters, who wished to abolish the calves, opposed him. Likewise, concerning Hoshea son of Elah, it says, “He did what was evil in the eyes of Hashem, but not like the kings of Israel who preceded him.” This indicates that he did not worship the calves. Our Sages likewise said that he abolished the guards Jeroboam had stationed along the roads to prevent Israel from making the pilgrimage to Jerusalem. The faction that remained attached to Jeroboam’s sin therefore opposed Hoshea and informed against him to the king of Assyria, who imprisoned him. Thus, these two kings were removed without My knowledge—that is, contrary to Hashem’s will.
text.7_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: From their silver and gold they made idols for themselves: While the kings supported the worship of the calves, the kings made the idols from the royal treasury. But when Shallum son of Jabesh and Hoshea son of Elah reigned and did not support the worship of the calves and idols, the people made idols for themselves from their own silver and gold, so that the king might be destroyed—the king whom they had initially appointed. They made the idols in order to strengthen the alliance of those who supported the worship of the calves and had conspired to destroy the king.
text.7_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: He rejected your calf, O Samaria: That is, “so that the king who rejected your calf might be destroyed”—the king who abandoned Samaria’s calf and refused to worship it. My anger burns against them: Until now, when the calves were made at the kings’ command, Hashem’s anger was directed primarily against the kings. But now that the king has rejected the calf while the people have made it from their own silver, the anger will henceforth be directed against them—the people. How long will they be incapable of innocence? How long will this sin of the calves remain among them, leaving them unable to cleanse themselves of it? They are no longer compelled to worship the calves and are now free to serve Hashem.
text.7_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: For it is from Israel: Until now, the calf had not been made with the people’s silver but with the king’s silver, and it was not they who made it, but the king. Now, however, it is from Israel, for they supplied the silver for it, as it says, “From their silver and gold they made idols for themselves.” Moreover, a craftsman made it—the artisan who fashioned the calf likewise came from Israel; it was not made by the king. The meaning of the verse is: For the calf of Samaria is from Israel, and a craftsman made it; it is not God, for they desire to be wayward. They do not worship it because they believe it to be God, but because they wish to behave rebelliously. They prefer lawlessness and therefore make the calves, which serve them as a symbol of abandoning restraint, casting off the yoke of Torah and the commandments, and becoming wayward so that they may follow every desire of their hearts. Therefore, they fashioned the calves even though they themselves know that they are not gods.
text.7_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: For they sow the wind: Therefore, they received recompense corresponding to their deeds. Just as they sowed wind, so they shall reap a whirlwind, which is greater than ordinary wind. It shall have no standing grain: The seed they sowed will produce no standing crop; that is, they will not enjoy the fruit of their labor. Nevertheless, even a shoot that can produce no flour, strangers will swallow it, lest perhaps it should produce some. That is, even something that begins to sprout from their labor, although it will never produce flour because it is only a thin shoot scorched by the east wind, will nevertheless be immediately swallowed and destroyed by strangers. For they will suspect that it might eventually produce flour once it matures. Therefore, they will not allow it to grow at all but will devour it immediately while it is still in its first growth. He now explains the allegory:
text.7_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Israel is swallowed up: Likewise, Israel has been swallowed up, for strangers have devoured him. Although he has now become among the nations like a vessel in which no one delights—like a shoot that will produce no flour—they nevertheless swallowed him up because he might perhaps produce flour in the future.
text.7_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: For: He explains what caused this. They subjected themselves to the kings of Assyria, but afterward betrayed their covenant and sent messengers to So, king of Egypt, seeking an alliance with him against Assyria. This aroused the fury of the king of Assyria against them (as explained above, 7:11). Thus he says, for they went up to Assyria and accepted its dominion over them. Afterward, Ephraim hired lovers: He gave payment to the king of Egypt, like a harlot who has a husband but pays other men to seek their love, abandon her husband, and rebel against him. He says, a wild donkey remains alone by itself. Even a wild donkey accustomed to the wilderness, which wanders far from its place—as it says (Jeremiah 2:24), “a wild donkey accustomed to the wilderness, sniffing the wind in the desire of its soul”—nevertheless travels alone despite its wanderings, for it shuns love and companionship and does not seek numerous companions. Ephraim, however, is different. Although he resembles a wild donkey in his conduct and likewise loves to wander from his place, he sought numerous allies and paid them to obtain their affection.
text.7_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Even so: Nevertheless, although they now give payments among the nations, paying the nations to obtain their affection and form alliances with them, there is still hope that I may gather them even now from the places to which they have been driven and restore their fortunes. This will occur if the king and the princes begin to tremble even slightly because of the prophetic burden—if their king and princes begin to fear, even a little, the burden of calamity that the prophets proclaimed against them. If they are moved even slightly by the prophets’ words and return to Hashem, I will gather them even now.
text.7_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: For: But they did not tremble at the burden of Hashem’s word, for Ephraim multiplied altars for sin. When they paid tribute among the nations, they did not merely offer payment for political alliances; they also joined the nations in worshiping their idols and multiplied altars upon which to sacrifice to the nations’ gods. His altars became altars for sin: In Ephraim’s view, the many altars he erected for idolatry were not sinful. Rather, the altars he had originally possessed for the service of Heaven were regarded by him as altars of sin. He now explains which altars he originally possessed:
text.7_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Though I wrote for him the great principles of My Torah: These include the altars prescribed in My Torah, meaning the altars made for offering sacrifices to Heaven—specifically, the altar in the Temple constructed according to the Torah. Yet these were regarded by them as something foreign. Anyone who went up to offer a sacrifice upon the Temple altar was killed. Likewise, anyone who built an altar for offerings to Heaven was considered a sinner, and they would kill him. For they maintained that the altars they had formerly possessed for the service of Heaven were sinful in their eyes.
text.7_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: The sacrifices destined for My flames: The burnt offerings consecrated to Heaven to be consumed entirely by the flame, they remove from their sacred status; they sacrifice them as ordinary meat and eat them. They turn them into ordinary sacrifices and consume the flesh, saying that Hashem does not desire them—that Hashem does not desire sacrifices because, in their view, He does not watch over human conduct, much less accept offerings from human beings. They therefore sacrifice to the Baals, the stars of heaven, and their constellations, while an offering brought to Hashem is regarded by them as sinful. All this explains the statement that they did not tremble at the burden of the prophets’ words. Not only this, but even now, when He remembers their iniquity and visits their sins by punishing them through the king of Assyria, they still do not tremble at Hashem’s punishments or return to Him. Instead, they shall return to Egypt: They went to Egypt, making it appear as though they were returning there. That is, it was as though Hashem had never redeemed them to become His people, but they were returning to what they had originally been in Egypt—idolaters who had never received the Torah and commandments.
text.7_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Israel forgot his Maker: There in Egypt, Israel forgot Hashem, who had made him into a people, and built temples, like the Egyptians, who were known to build a separate temple for each star in which to worship that particular star. And Judah, although serving Hashem in the Temple, multiplied fortified cities, placing his trust in the strength of his fortifications rather than in Hashem. Therefore, I will send fire into his cities, etc.
text.8_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not rejoice, O Israel: You, Israel, cannot rejoice with exultation like the other nations. The nations are subject to the celestial order, as it says, “which Hashem your God allotted to all the peoples.” When their constellation grants them success and the celestial order favors them, they rejoice. But you are not subject to the stars of heaven and their constellations, for you are betrothed to Hashem, as it says, “Your Maker is your Husband; Hashem of Hosts is His name.” When you depart from His Providence to worship other gods, you resemble a wife who commits harlotry against her husband. Thus He says, for you have strayed in harlotry from your God; you have loved payment. You resemble a harlot who loves payment and therefore wanders upon every threshing floor of grain to commit harlotry there and receive her payment. Likewise, you wander from nation to nation seeking your sustenance there.
text.8_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Threshing floor: For the threshing floor and the winepress that they possessed in their own land—the sustenance allotted to her by her Husband at the time of their marriage—will not sustain them. They will no longer obtain their sustenance from the threshing floors of their land, and the new wine will fail her in the land mentioned below. Grain and new wine will no longer be found there as in former times, for:
text.8_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: They shall not dwell in Hashem’s land: They will be exiled from the land because of their sins, and the land will become desolate. Consequently, Ephraim shall return to Egypt to settle there, and in Assyria, to which they will be exiled, they shall eat unclean bread among the nations. The wine had been blessed through the merit of those dwelling in the Land. Now, however, the new wine will fail in the Land because they will no longer dwell there. Moreover, the wine had been blessed on account of the libations they offered, as our Sages taught, but this too will no longer occur, for:
text.8_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: They shall not pour out wine to Hashem: Not only will they cease to bring libations, which are secondary to the sacrifice, but their sacrifices will not be acceptable to Him either, for sacrifices were called “the bread of Hashem,” as it says, “For they offer Hashem’s fire-offerings, the bread of their God,” and were holy. Their sacrifices, however, will not be called Hashem’s bread, for they shall be like the bread of mourners to them. They resemble the food eaten by those mourning their dead, who partake of the meal of consolation provided by others. Likewise, the peace offerings they eat will not be offerings of rejoicing but a meal of consolation. Whereas ordinary mourners’ bread is defiled by the mourner, who has become impure through contact with the dead and thereby contaminates the bread, concerning the bread of their sacrifices, all who eat it shall become impure—the bread itself will defile those who consume it. For their bread is for their own dead soul: It is bread they eat on account of their own dead soul, for their soul has died within their body, and they consume the sacrifice as a meal of consolation over their own death. Therefore, it shall not enter the house of Hashem, for it is impure bread.
text.8_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: What will you do? This refers back to the statement, “Do not rejoice, O Israel, with exultation like the nations.” How will you seek to rejoice on the day of an appointed festival, when the nations celebrated their festivals during the barley and wheat harvests and at the time of the ingathering? How will you rejoice with exultation when the threshing floor and winepress will not sustain you? Likewise, what will you do on the day of Hashem’s festival? On the festivals, they offered sacrifices and poured wine libations. Once the sacrifices and libations have ceased, with what will you celebrate Hashem’s festival?
text.8_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: For behold, they have gone away from the breast: This corresponds to the statement, “Ephraim shall return to Egypt.” Israel imagined that they were returning to the land of their birth, since the nation had first come into being in Egypt. They viewed themselves as one returning to his native land, where he had nursed at his mother’s breasts—returning to his mother’s breast and the chamber where he was conceived. The prophet therefore says that this is a false image. In truth, the Land of Israel is their mother’s breast: there they nursed honey and milk, and it is the land of their birth, as it says, “They shall mourn over the breasts” (Isaiah 33). Now that they have been exiled from their land, behold, they have departed from their mother’s breast. They resemble one leaving the land of his birth for the land of his burial, for they are going to Egypt to die and be buried there. Egypt shall gather them so that Memphis may bury them, for there will be their burial place. And who will inherit their property and wealth? Nettles shall inherit what was precious among their silver, and thorns shall dwell within their tents, which will remain desolate.
text.8_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: They have come: Until now, they did not know Hashem or believe His prophets, who foretold the punishments that would come upon them from Him. But once the days of reckoning have come, when Hashem visits their sins, and the days of repayment have come, when the prophets’ words are fulfilled and He repays them according to their deeds, then Israel shall know that the prophets’ words were true. Until now, the prophet was a fool in your eyes: the prophet who foretold what would befall you was regarded by you as a foolish man, and the man of spirit was considered insane. This was because of the greatness of your iniquity—because you deliberately acted perversely and refused to believe the one who rebuked you for your sin. Therefore, the hostility was great.
text.8_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: The watchman: That is, great was your hostility toward Ephraim’s watchman, who stood with my God. You bore intense hostility toward the watchman who foretold calamity for you, and also toward the God who sent him to prophesy, for you hated both Hashem and His prophets. Thus, whenever a prophet prophesied to you in Hashem’s name, you prepared a fowler’s snare upon all his paths, setting traps to capture and kill him, as it says, “They dug a pit to capture me and concealed snares for my feet.” Moreover, there was hostility in the house of his God: Hostility toward the prophet was found even within the house of God, for Zechariah was killed in the Temple, and even the house of Hashem did not protect him.
text.8_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: They have sunk deeply: Beyond all this, they have sunk deeply in attempting to conceal their plans from Hashem, and they have corrupted their ways through sexual immorality, as they did in the days of Gibeah, when their deeds resembled those of Sodom. Thus, they are evil toward Hashem and also sinful in their conduct toward other people. Therefore, He will remember their iniquity and punish them for it.
text.8_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Like grapes: Regarding the statement that they had corrupted their ways through idolatry and sexual immorality, as in the days of Gibeah, and that He would therefore remember their iniquity, he says that they should draw an argument from the lesser to the greater from the punishment inflicted upon those who left Egypt for the sin of Baal-peor and their sexual immorality with the daughters of Moab. That generation was esteemed and precious in Hashem’s eyes, yet He punished them; all the more, then, will He punish these people, who are base and contemptible in His eyes, for the same sins. He says: I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. When I found Israel in the wilderness, they were as precious to Me as grapes found in a desert—a place where neither seed, vine, nor fig tree normally grows—since grapes are the most valued fruit one could find there. That is, Israel was the first vineyard planted by Hashem, as it says, “You brought a vine out of Egypt.” Grapevines do not accept grafting, especially grapes growing in the wilderness, which are ungrafted. Likewise, Israel was then holy and guarded against sexual immorality, as our Sages taught that Shelomith daughter of Dibri was the sole exception, and Scripture publicized her identity. Similarly, I saw your fathers like the first-ripening fig on the fig tree in its earliest season. The fig too is an especially valuable fruit and contains no refuse, while the first fig to ripen is particularly precious because fruit is still scarce at that time. Israel was therefore precious both because of the place, like grapes in the wilderness, and because of the time: the Divine influence first rested upon them while darkness still covered the earth and thick darkness covered the nations. Nevertheless, although they were exceedingly precious to Me, they came to Baal-peor, etc., through their love. That is, even they, despite all their distinction, through their love—when they loved the daughters of Moab—descended from one degradation to another. This love brought them to Baal-peor, as it says, “The people began to commit harlotry with the daughters of Moab,” and consequently, “they invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods.” Thereby, they consecrated themselves to the shameful thing, as it says, “The people ate and bowed down to their gods.” Consequently, they became detestable, for Hashem regarded them as abominable and rejected them, as it says, “Hashem’s anger burned against Israel.” All this occurred through their love for the daughters of Moab. Now reason from the lesser to the greater: if they became detestable through loving the daughters of Moab, despite having originally been so precious, then all the more so—
text.8_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Ephraim, whose glory shall fly away like a bird—from birth, from the womb, and from conception: They possessed neither honor nor distinction even at the beginning of their existence. At their birth, while still in their mother’s womb, and even from the time of their conception, they had no honor at all, for most of them were illegitimate children conceived through harlotry. All the more, then, will their own harlotry make them detestable in My eyes.
text.8_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: For: Ephraim has two deficiencies in comparison with the generation of the wilderness. First, even if they raise their children, I will bereave them of mankind—their children are not regarded by Me as possessing the status of human beings at all. They have been detestable from the womb, like base and loathsome animals, because they did not preserve the purity of their lineage and begot illegitimate children. Second, woe also to them—even to the parents of those children who were not conceived through harlotry and are therefore included among human beings—woe to them when I withdraw from them. Although I was originally with them, I have now departed from them and cast them away from My presence because of their evil deeds.
text.8_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Ephraim: He adds that Ephraim does not resemble the first generation, who were like grapes found in the wilderness. Ephraim does not dwell in a wilderness but resembles Tyre, planted in a pleasant habitation. I transplanted him from the wilderness and planted him in an inhabited dwelling—that is, he possesses a settled land, and I saw him securely established in his country amid abundant prosperity, like Tyre. Nevertheless, he corrupted his conduct so severely that it was decreed that Ephraim must bring forth his children to the murderer, although according to nature they should have succeeded, multiplied, and been fruitful in the good and spacious land I gave them.
text.8_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Give them: The prophet turns toward Hashem and prays that He not exile them. He says, Give them, O Hashem—what will You give? That is, give them the punishment appropriate for the sin of adultery, as it is Your way to punish measure for measure. For the sin of sexual immorality, it is fitting that You give them a miscarrying womb and shriveled breasts, so that they will be unable to beget children of harlotry, unable to raise them, and unable to multiply illegitimate offspring. This is the appropriate punishment—not exile and expulsion from their land, which is not measure for measure.
text.8_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: All: Hashem answers him: The exile is not imposed solely because of the sin of sexual immorality, for this is only a portion of their wickedness. Rather, all their wickedness is found in Gilgal. There they committed other evils—idolatry, murder, and additional abominations besides sexual immorality. For there I hated them because of the wickedness of their deeds—the other abominations found among them. Therefore, I will drive them from My house. I no longer desire them to remain in My house, meaning the Land I gave them in which to dwell. This resembles a man who hates his wife because of her wicked conduct and drives her from his home, no longer providing her with either shelter or sustenance. There is no hope that I will again be reconciled with them, for I will no longer love them. There is no prospect that they will improve their conduct, since all their princes are rebellious and lead them away from the proper path.
text.8_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Stricken: Nor is it necessary for Me to give them a miscarrying womb so that they will bear no fruit, for this has occurred by itself. Ephraim himself has struck his root, so that it has dried up and they shall bear no fruit. He has become like a tree whose root has withered and which is naturally incapable of producing fruit, even without a punishment imposed through Divine Providence. Beyond this, even if they happen to give birth, I will put to death the cherished fruit of their womb as a punishment through Divine Providence.
text.8_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: My God will reject them: God will reject them personally because they did not listen to Him, and they shall become wanderers among the nations. Therefore, it was decreed that they be exiled from their land to the lands of the nations.
text.9_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: A vine: After stating that an irrevocable decree had been issued that they would go into exile, he explains how events developed so that they were exiled from their land. Hashem cast confusion and rebellion among them, causing them to revolt against their kings, and this brought about their exile. I have already explained (above, chapters 7 and 8) that their rebellion against Shallum son of Jabesh, whom they killed, and later against Hoshea son of Elah, whom they denounced to the king of Assyria for sending messengers to So, king of Egypt, resulted from the fact that these two kings did not adhere to the sin of Jeroboam and sought to abolish the worship of the calves. Consequently, the faction attached to the worship of the calves rose against them. This caused the king of Assyria to invade them first during the days of Menahem son of Gadi and finally during the days of Hoshea, when he exiled them all. Concerning these events, the prophet delivers an exalted vision and metaphor in this chapter. He says, Israel is an emptying vine. Israel is compared to a vine, as it says, “My beloved had a vineyard on a fertile hill.” Hashem planted this vine and hoped that it would produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes, as stated in Isaiah, chapter 5. There it explains, “He hoped for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry.” Thus, the fruit Hashem expected this vine to produce was justice and righteousness. But Israel is an emptying vine that empties itself and sheds the fruit fitting for it—the fruit it ought to produce. For as his fruit increased, he multiplied altars for idolatry, and as his land prospered, they made their sacred pillars more splendid for idol worship.
text.9_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Divided: Therefore, Hashem divided their heart, causing dissension among them and the formation of opposing factions. Consequently, they shall now bear their guilt—that is, through this division they will receive their punishment—for it will break the necks of their altars: this division of heart will destroy their altars and devastate their sacred pillars. That is, the king who replaced his predecessor would destroy the altars of the calves, as Shallum son of Jabesh and Hoshea son of Elah did, and this would provoke a rebellion against the king.
text.9_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: For now they will say, “We have no king”: Consequently, they will rebel against their king and seek to remove him from the throne. For we do not fear Hashem: They will say that they do not accept the king’s attempt to abolish the worship of the calves and replace it with the worship of Hashem, because they do not fear Hashem and do not desire either reverence for Him or His service. If so, what can the king do to us? How can the king compel us to serve Hashem and fear Him? This will cause them to rebel against their king. This also explains the statement, Their heart is divided; now they shall bear their guilt. Through this division of heart, the guilt of the calves will henceforth rest upon the people themselves. Until then, the guilt had rested upon the kings, who compelled the people to worship the calves. But now that the king sought to abolish the calves while the people insisted upon retaining them, they themselves will bear the guilt, which will rest upon their own heads rather than upon those of their kings.
text.9_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: They spoke words: Thus they spoke words of rebellion among themselves, swearing false oaths. They thereby violated the oath they had sworn to remain loyal to their king, claiming that this oath had no validity once he sought to abolish the worship of the calves. They made a covenant: They entered into a covenant with one another to carry out their rebellious conspiracy—either to kill Shallum or to deliver Hoshea into the hands of the king of Assyria so that he would destroy him. Then judgment sprang up like a poisonous plant in the furrows of the field: Their punishment immediately began to sprout. The seed of rebellion, which they had secretly sown within the deep furrows of their hearts, germinated, blossomed, and produced clusters of bitter fruit. The judgment of their punishment then sprang up openly like poison and wormwood in the furrows of a field, and they immediately received their punishment, as he will explain.
text.9_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: For the calf: He now explains in detail what caused the rebellion concerning which he said, “They spoke words, swearing false oaths,” and how judgment and punishment immediately began to sprout. The rebellion arose because of the calf of Beth-Aven—the calf at Bethel. On its account, the inhabitants of Samaria gathered together to rebel against their king because he had abolished its worship. For its people mourned over it, as did its idolatrous priests, who had formerly rejoiced over the calf but now mourned and grieved because its glory had departed from it. Hoshea son of Elah had abolished the calf’s honored status and permitted the people to make the pilgrimage to Jerusalem and serve Hashem. This was the cause of the rebellion.
text.9_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: It too: He now explains the statement, “Judgment sprang up like a poisonous plant,” showing how they immediately received their punishment. When the king of Assyria seized Hoshea, detained him, and imprisoned him, he also took the calf. Thus, it too shall be carried to Assyria: Not only was the king taken to Assyria, but the calf as well was carried there as tribute to the contentious king. Assyria shall take Ephraim’s shame: Assyria will take away that which brought shame upon Ephraim—namely, its calf, which was a source of disgrace and humiliation to Ephraim. Therefore, Israel shall be ashamed of its counsel—the plan to rebel against Hoshea and deliver him into Assyria’s hands, through which they imagined they would restore the worship of the calf to its former standing. Instead, their scheme caused the calf’s worship to be abolished completely.
text.9_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Destroyed: He explains how Israel will be ashamed of its counsel. Through that counsel, Samaria’s king was destroyed like foam upon the surface of water. When the waters boil, rage, and churn in the depths, foam and froth form upon their surface. Afterward, that foam drifts away and disappears through the action of the water itself, which does not remain in a single state. Likewise, the king arose through the people’s agitation, fury, and rebellion against their previous king. They conspired together with Hoshea against Pekah son of Remaliah, killed Pekah, and made Hoshea king in his place. Afterward, this foam drifted away into exile because of the people’s denunciation and their continually changing opinions, for their hearts never remained in one state. Yet when their scheme caused the king to be led in chains to Assyria, they did not accomplish their intended plan of strengthening the worship of the calf. On the contrary:
text.9_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And they shall be destroyed: Through this, the high places of wickedness, which were the sin of Israel, shall also be destroyed. From then on, thorns and thistles shall grow upon their altars, for they will become desolate and ruined. The altars standing upon the mountains and hills will say, “Mountains, cover us,” and “Hills, fall upon us.” Because of the profound desolation, the mountains and hills will collapse over the altars, covering and burying them beneath heaps of earth. Thus, their counsel was plainly foolish and accomplished nothing.
text.9_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Since the days of Gibeah, Israel has sinned: The high places of wickedness and Israel’s sin—idolatry—were already present among Israel in the days of Gibeah. Even then, they had established Micah’s idol at Dan. Jeroboam therefore placed one of his calves at Dan because that location had already been established as a place of idol worship in ancient times. Thus He says, there they remained: The high places and idols had remained there at Dan since ancient times. Our Sages already explained that Israel did not succeed in its first two battles against Gibeah, although they displayed zeal for Hashem over the sexual outrage, because they had not displayed similar zeal against Micah’s idol. Thus He says, the war at Gibeah against the children of wickedness did not overtake them. The war they fought at Gibeah against the evildoers—the Benjaminites—did not reach the high places of Micah’s idol, for those high places remained standing and were not abolished at that time. This demonstrates that Israel had already begun turning toward idolatry and therefore displayed no zeal against it.
text.9_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: When I desire, I will chastise them: Therefore, when I desired to chastise and punish them for the sin of idolatry, I did not assemble a force from among Israel to wage war against the sinners, for Israel had displayed no zeal against idolatry even then, much less now. Instead, the nations shall be gathered against them—the Assyrian army will assemble against them—when they are bound to their two furrows. The Assyrians will bind them to the two furrows of their plow: they will place a heavy yoke upon them and bind them with restraints, as one harnesses a plowing ox and forces it to plow two furrows at once—twice what its strength can bear. That is, they will be compelled to labor beyond their capacity.
text.9_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Ephraim is a trained heifer: Ephraim lacks the strength of an ox that bears a yoke and plows the soil. He resembles a young calf trained to perform light labor, which loves to thresh. She loves threshing grain, the work suited to a calf: it treads upon the grain, threshes it, and also eats while threshing. But plowing is not the work of a tender calf. That is, Ephraim prefers to bear a light subjugation, such as the rule of the king of Egypt, which would have imposed a mild yoke and easy service, while allowing them to eat from Egypt’s prosperity and profit from commerce there. Ephraim does not wish to bear the yoke of the king of Assyria, plowing and laboring under crushing servitude. But I passed over her fine neck: I still had compassion upon her, for I passed by and observed her fine, fat, and delicate neck, which was incapable of bearing a heavy yoke. I therefore still intended not to deliver her to the nations, who would bind her with restraints and force her to plow two furrows at once. I thought that they would submit their necks to My service, which is a light service, and would thereby avoid being delivered into the hands of a harsh master. I intended that they join the kingdom of Judah, so that both kingdoms would serve Hashem and cultivate His soil—the holy soil—together. Thus, I thought, I will harness Ephraim: I will join and attach him to Judah so that the two will plow and labor together in Hashem’s field. I hoped that Judah would plow, while Jacob would harrow for himself. Judah, who is accustomed to plowing through the service of Hashem, would perform the plowing, which is the more difficult labor. Jacob, meaning the Ten Tribes, who is not accustomed to plowing the soil, would perform the harrowing—the lighter labor done after plowing, when one passes over the furrows again to crush the clods. That is, Judah would prepare the soil of the soul, plowing it until it was ready to receive the seed of righteousness and good deeds. Jacob, the Ten Tribes, would then follow and complete the plowing and preparation. Then:
text.9_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Sow righteousness for yourselves: Then you will sow righteousness and good deeds through the commandments governing the relationship between a person and God. Reap according to kindness: Just as one planted seed produces many harvested sheaves, so the reward they receive will accord with Hashem’s kindness, exceeding the recompense strictly deserved according to truth and justice. It will be kindness without limit or measure. He adds, Plow for yourselves virgin soil: This means digging deeply into the earth to remove the thorns that destroy the crop. Likewise, you must dig into the depths of the soul to remove the desires, corrupt thoughts, and false beliefs that destroy the seeds of righteousness and good deeds.
text.9_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: And it is time to seek Hashem: After they prepare the ground through plowing and sowing, the season of rain will arrive. They must then seek Hashem and request His presence, asking Him to provide the early and latter rains in their proper seasons. That is, they must ask Him for heavenly bounty and Divine assistance from above, until He comes and showers upon you—until He comes to you and provides the early rain. He explains what this rain will be: He will shower righteousness upon you. The righteousness He sends will itself be the rain He provides. This shows that he does not refer literally to earthly soil, but to the soil of their souls. He will satisfy their thirsty souls with His mighty rains and holy bounty, as it says, “Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness.”
text.9_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: You have plowed: But you have plowed wickedness, and therefore you have reaped injustice and eaten the fruit of falsehood. That is, you consumed the fruits of your falsehood and denial of Hashem. This occurred because you trusted in your own way and in the multitude of your warriors, imagining that strategy and military strength would save you.
text.9_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And a tumult shall arise: When a tumult and rebellion arose among your peoples, as they rebelled against their king, consequently all your fortresses were plundered. Through the internal conflict among them, they delivered their strongholds into the enemy’s hands, as in Shalman’s destruction, when Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, destroyed Beth-arbel, a fortress within the kingdom of Ephraim, on the day of battle. On that day, they delivered the fortress into his hands because of the rebellion and strife among themselves. He also calls it “Shalman’s destruction” because they surrendered the fortress to him peacefully, yet he treated its inhabitants as though he had captured them through an ambush in battle and conquered them by force. Then the mother was dashed to pieces upon her children, for he killed the entire population as though he had taken them through a violent conquest.
text.9_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus has Bethel done to you: Bethel caused all this to befall you, for the calf at Bethel was the cause of everything. Because of the wickedness of your wickedness: This calamity came through your own wickedness. Your evil conduct brought evil upon you; because of your wicked deeds, disaster befell you. Thus, at dawn the king of Israel was utterly destroyed. You rebelled against the king, and through this he was silenced and cut off. He was destroyed at dawn; yet together with the king, the dawn itself was also extinguished—the star of your prosperity. From that moment onward, the morning star was darkened for you. All this resulted from Bethel, where the rebellion arose because the king sought to abolish the calf at Bethel, as explained above.
text.10_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: When Israel was a youth: When Israel was still a tender young child—that is, in Egypt—I loved him, and from Egypt I called My son. At that time, although he did not call upon Me, I called him lovingly to come to Me, like a father who loves his son and calls him to come near even though the son does not call for his father.
text.10_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: They called to them: The Baals whom they worship, however, are the opposite: Israel calls to them, yet the Baals depart from their presence and distance themselves from them. He explains to whom “they called”: to the Baals, to whom they sacrifice, and to the idols, to which they burn incense. Israel calls out to the Baals, but they remain far from them.
text.10_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: But I supported Ephraim upon his feet: I am Ephraim’s support—that is, I am the footstool upon which Ephraim stands and the foundation that carries him. He takes them upon his arms: This means that I support Ephraim while he takes the Baals upon his arms. He depicts Ephraim lifting the Baals and carrying them in his arms, while he himself, together with the Baals he carries, stands upon Me; I am his support and the place beneath the soles of his feet. For the Baals must be carried by their worshipers, whereas I carry My creatures. But they did not know that I healed them: When they recover from their illnesses, they imagine that the Baal they carry has healed them. They do not recognize that I—not the idol—am the healer and deliverer.
text.10_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: I drew them with human cords: On the one hand, I drew them with “human cords”—that is, I brought a man against them, namely Assyria, who bound them with cords and drew them beneath the yoke of his burdensome service.
