On the other hand, I drew them with bonds of love, drawing them toward Me to remain under My authority and Providence because of My love for them. Thus, I drew them with bonds, which are stronger than the cords with which a human being draws them toward himself. He explains how He drew them with bonds of love: I was to them like one who lifts the yoke from their jaws, relieving them of the burden’s yoke, and I bent down to him with food. This resembles one who has compassion upon an animal laboring beneath a yoke. The yoke weighs heavily upon it and also prevents it from reaching the food lying on the ground. He therefore lifts the yoke so that it will not burden the animal and brings the food close to its mouth so that it need not bend down to the ground.
text.10_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: He shall not return: He explains that Hashem wished to lighten their yoke. Although their sins required them to remain under the rule of the king of Assyria, the Assyrian king would not have made their yoke so burdensome had they not rebelled against him by sending messengers to So, king of Egypt. This caused the king of Assyria to become enraged with them and exile them, as explained above (7:11; 8:9). Thus He says: I warned and advised him not to return to the land of Egypt by sending messengers there, since Assyria is his king, because they refused to return. Since their refusal to return to Hashem compelled them to serve Assyria—for this had been decreed upon them because of their sins—Assyria was now their king. It was therefore improper for them to violate their covenant by turning back toward Egypt and rebelling against the king of Assyria.
text.10_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And the sword shall whirl against his cities: They did not listen to My advice but resolved to send messengers to the king of Egypt. Consequently, the king of Assyria came against them and exiled them. Therefore, when the sword whirled against his cities, consumed his branches, and devoured everything, I was not responsible for what occurred. It resulted from their own counsels, for through their evil plan they brought all this upon themselves by refusing to accept My advice.
text.10_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And My people hang expectantly upon My return: The prophet presents an exalted image. He depicts the king of Assyria conquering Samaria and seeking to destroy and annihilate everyone. Hashem has withdrawn from them and is ascending toward His dwelling in heaven, yet He has not completely distanced Himself and still stands between earth and heaven. Because of their sins, He wishes to withdraw into the highest heavens; yet because of His compassion and kindness, He also desires not to distance Himself from them. At that moment of distress, Israel raises its eyes toward Hashem and waits for Him to return and rescue them. Thus He says, My people hang expectantly upon My return: Their eyes are raised toward heaven, hoping that I will return to them in their distress. At the very least, they ask that I not withdraw still higher, so that I may remain near them. Thus, the meaning of the verse is: They all call to Him together, asking that He not ascend on high. All Israel calls to Him and asks that He not raise His Divine Presence into the highest heavens and withdraw from them completely. This corresponds to what was stated above (5:15): “I will depart and return to My place until they acknowledge their guilt and seek My face.” Accordingly, he depicts them in their time of distress, as Hashem prepares to return to His dwelling, seeking His presence and asking Him not to distance Himself from them but to remain ready to save them.
text.10_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: How? This is Hashem’s response. He now depicts, on the one hand, how Hashem, in His abundant compassion, desires to return to the city of Samaria, knowing that if He withdraws into the highest heavens, the king of Assyria will annihilate them and leave neither survivor nor remnant. On the other hand, He depicts Hashem as unable to return to the city because Samaria’s wickedness has become as great as that of Sodom and Gomorrah. When Hashem descended to Sodom and Gomorrah, He overturned them in His anger and fury, as it says, “I will descend now and see whether they have acted entirely according to the outcry that has come before Me.” This occurred through His sending His angels there; once they entered the city, they were compelled to overturn it. Likewise, if Hashem descends into the city of Samaria, He will be compelled to overturn it because of its wickedness. Thus, He does not know what to do: if He does not return to the city, it will be overturned by the king of Assyria; but if He returns to the city and rescues it from the king of Assyria, it will be overturned by Hashem Himself. Thus He says, on the one hand, I desire to return to Samaria, for how can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I deliver you into the enemy’s hands and allow him to annihilate you? Yet on the other hand, I cannot return to the city, for how can I make you like Admah and set you like Zeboiim? If I descend into the city, I will have to overturn it by an act of Heaven, as Sodom, Admah, and Zeboiim were overturned when I entered among them. Thus, I do not know what to do. On the one hand, My heart has turned within Me—My heart has turned favorably toward them, desiring to protect them from the fury of the king of Assyria, and therefore I wish to descend. On the other hand, My consolations have together grown fervent: If I seek to relent from the calamity I decreed upon them through the king of Assyria and descend into the city to rescue them, My attempt to relent becomes inflamed, for I will then be compelled to destroy the city Myself, as I destroyed Admah and Zeboiim.
text.10_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: I will not carry it out: Accordingly, Hashem says that He chose an intermediate course. He would not withdraw to His heavenly dwelling and abandon them helplessly to the king of Assyria, allowing him to annihilate them according to the decree initially issued in His burning anger. Thus He says, I will not carry out My fierce anger. Yet neither would He return to dwell with them in the city of Samaria, for then He would be compelled to destroy them as God destroyed the cities of the plain. Thus He says, I will not return—I will not return to the city of Samaria—because then I would be compelled to destroy Ephraim. For I am God and not a man. This explains both statements. Because I am God and am gracious, I will not carry out My fierce anger. Yet because I am God, I cannot return to Samaria after they have acted like Sodom and Gomorrah, for I would then be compelled to destroy them. Hashem therefore chose an intermediate course: He would not distance Himself from them by withdrawing into heaven, but would descend to remain among them and protect them. Nevertheless, He would not enter the city of Samaria. Instead, He would remain outside the city and bring them out of it to go into exile. Hashem would proceed before the exiles, and they would follow Him. Thus He says: I have therefore resolved that the Holy One shall remain in your midst—I will remain holy among you and will not distance Myself from you—yet I will not enter the city of Samaria. Instead, I will bring them outside the city. Then:
text.10_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: They shall follow Hashem: Once they are outside the city, they will find Hashem prepared to go at the head of the exiles, and they will follow Him. He will remain holy in their midst, watching over them in exile so that the king of Assyria does not annihilate them. He shall roar like a lion: He informs them, however, that when He proceeds before them into exile, He will not make His own voice heard as the voice of the Almighty, but will roar with the voice of a lion. The metaphor is that the kingdom of Assyria, and likewise the Babylonian kingdom that afterward assumed its dominion, was represented by the form of a lion. Thus Daniel saw in his vision, “The first was like a lion,” referring to the kingdom of Babylon. Ezekiel similarly saw its heavenly prince in the Divine chariot with the face of a lion, as I explained there. Likewise, it says, “A lion has risen from its thicket,” and below (13:7), “I became to them like a lion.” Hashem says that in exile He will clothe Himself in the heavenly prince of the nation that exiled His children, thereby assuming the form of a lion and roaring like a lion. That is, He will not make His own mighty voice heard by performing open miracles. Instead, He will incline the hearts of the king and his princes favorably toward Israel and watch over them through concealed Providence, so that it will appear as though the lion is roaring and the king himself is governing them benevolently and showing them favor. Hashem’s Providence will operate through the lion’s roar—that is, through the influence of the nation’s heavenly prince and the conduct of its king and officers. Through this voice He will roar to save them.
text.10_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: For He Himself shall roar: Yet a time will come when He Himself shall roar—He will no longer roar like a lion but will make His own voice, the voice of God, heard by performing wonders for them as in ancient times. Then the children shall hasten trembling from the west: The children of the living God who are exiled in the western lands will then hasten to leave their exile.
text.10_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Likewise, they shall hasten like a bird to depart from Egypt, and they shall hasten like a dove to leave the land of Assyria. Certain species of dove can recognize their home from a very great distance. Likewise, even those lost in the land of Assyria—who are called “lost” because they have been driven so far away, as stated in Isaiah 27—will hasten to return to their nest. Then I will settle them in their homes and bring them back to the Land of Israel.
text.11_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: They surrounded Me: Ephraim, the ruling tribe, surrounded Me with falsehood—the denial through which they rejected the foundations of faith and said to the calves, “These are your gods, O Israel.”
text.11_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: And the house of Israel with deceit: The other tribes practiced deceit in their dealings with one another, cheating and defrauding, as he will explain: “Canaan has deceitful scales in his hand.” But Judah still rules with God: In the days of Jotham and Hezekiah, they ruled in fear of Hashem regarding matters of faith.
text.11_Chapter, 0_Verse, 2_Comment: And he is faithful with the holy ones: Faithfulness is the opposite of deceit. Judah associates with the holy ones in practicing faithfulness, and they do not deceive one another.
text.11_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Ephraim: Ephraim, however, feeds upon wind and emptiness in matters of faith, and continually multiplies falsehood and violence in matters between one person and another. And a covenant: Beyond this, he prepares his own trap that will cause him to be exiled from his land. For after they made a covenant with Assyria and Hoshea became the Assyrian king’s vassal, why was oil carried to Egypt? Why did he send messengers to So, king of Egypt, which amounted to rebellion against the king of Assyria? This caused their exile, as the prophet already complained above (7:11; 8:9; 11:5).
text.11_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And there is a dispute concerning Hashem with Judah: That is, Ephraim contends with Judah in a dispute that concerns Hashem. During those days, conflict existed between Ephraim and Judah, and its cause was that Judah served Hashem and maintained the Temple service and its sacrifices, whereas Ephraim clung to Jeroboam’s sin and quarreled over Hashem. Ephraim conducted this dispute with Judah, and it too contributed to his downfall. Consequently, not only did Judah fail to assist Ephraim in its distress, but in the days of Ahaz, Judah even incited the king of Assyria against him. And to visit upon Jacob according to his ways: The Ten Tribes identified themselves by the name Jacob. Wherever this book refers simply to “the house of Jacob,” it means the Ten Tribes; similarly, wherever Israel and Judah are mentioned together, “Israel” refers to the Ten Tribes. Accordingly, regarding both Ephraim’s dispute with Judah and its rebellion against Hashem through worshiping the calves, the prophet says figuratively and ironically that they appear to be attempting to visit upon Jacob according to his ways—that is, to imitate Jacob. Regarding their fraternal conflict with their brother Judah, they might claim that Jacob had acted similarly, for:
text.11_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: In the womb he seized his brother by the heel: They likewise seize the heel of their brother Judah. Regarding their consecration of Bethel for the worship of the calves, he says, and by his strength he contended with God; he contended with an angel, etc. Through this, the prophet reveals an ancient mystery. We find that when Jeroboam became king, it says (I Kings 12:25), “Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and he went out from there and built Penuel. Then the king took counsel, made two golden calves, placed one in Bethel, and put the other in Dan.” We are not surprised that he placed one calf in Dan, for Micah’s idol had stood there since ancient times, and they believed that the place had thereby been consecrated for the worship of the calf. But why did he place the other calf specifically in Bethel? We have already explained that the calf at Bethel was the principal one in his eyes. Why, then, did he choose Bethel, and why did he build those two cities, Shechem and Penuel? All this can be understood through the fact that the Ten Tribes identified themselves with Jacob and sought to imitate him. When Jeroboam schemed to consecrate places that Israel would regard as holy like Jerusalem, he considered the journeys of Jacob, father of the nation. Jacob wrestled with the angel at Penuel, as it says, “He called the name of the place Peniel.” From Penuel he traveled to the city of Shechem, and from Shechem he journeyed to Bethel, where he built an altar. Jeroboam therefore built Shechem and Penuel because these places possessed sanctity: Penuel because Jacob first saw the angel there, and Shechem because Jacob later dwelt there and built an altar. At Bethel, however, God revealed Himself to Jacob. A Midrashic tradition relates that when the angel asked Jacob to release him and Jacob demanded that he confirm the blessing, the angel pleaded that Jacob release him for the present, promising that at Bethel he would confirm the blessing. This was an ancient tradition. On this basis, Jeroboam claimed that this angel had remained at Bethel and would reveal himself there to the prophets and worshipers of the calf. The prophet thus explains how, in their own view, they imitated Jacob in two respects. First, their conflict with their brother Judah resembled Jacob’s conflict with Esau. Second, by his strength Jacob contended with God; he contended with an angel and prevailed, as it says, “For you have contended with God and with men and have prevailed.” Then the angel wept and pleaded with him—with Jacob—and promised him that at Bethel he would find him and there confirm the blessings. On this basis, Ephraim now says, there he speaks with us. That is, the angel remains there even now and speaks with the descendants of Jacob—the worshipers of the calves at Bethel. They claimed that this angel would prophesy to them and serve as the intermediary who bestowed his blessings upon them even in the present.
text.11_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: But Hashem is the God of Hosts: The prophet responds to them: The Children of Israel do not receive their Divine bounty from an angel or heavenly prince; they receive it directly from Hashem, without any intermediary. Hashem is the God of Hosts—He rules over all the angelic hosts. Hashem is His memorial: Among us, He is remembered by the Divine Name signifying His essential existence, not by the title “Hosts,” nor by the name of any angel or heavenly prince. Why, then, do you place your trust in an angel or in one of the heavenly princes governing the celestial order? For surely:
text.11_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, return through your God: The condition for returning to your proper spiritual level is that you return through your God, the God of Israel—not through an angel. This will be accomplished by observing kindness and justice. Therefore, hope continually in your God, not in an angel or heavenly prince.
text.11_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Canaan: Until now, he has explained the statement, Ephraim has surrounded Me with falsehood, describing their denial and heresy—how they denied individual Divine Providence and worshiped the heavenly princes governing the celestial order. He now explains the statement, and the house of Israel with deceit, referring to their sins of fraud and exploitation in dealings between one person and another. The Canaanite—the merchant engaged in trade—holds deceitful scales in his hand because he loves to exploit.
text.11_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And Ephraim said: Ephraim claims that this is not a sin, since he does not rob by force but profits through commercial deception, by means of his own labor and the work of his hands. He says, Surely I have become wealthy through this, and I have acquired wealth for myself through my trade. Although I possessed differing weights for buying and selling, this is not a sin, for in all my earnings, they will find in me no iniquity that is sinful. Since I obtained this wealth through labor in commerce, my use of deceitful scales is not considered a sin.
text.11_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: But I: Hashem answers him: Am I not Hashem your God since the land of Egypt? The Exodus from Egypt is mentioned in the Torah concerning both interest and dishonest weights. In Egypt they were poor and, because of their poverty, had no money to lend at interest. Nor did they possess deceitful scales, for they engaged in no commerce. Therefore, in both these prohibitions, the Torah reminds them of the day they left Egypt, warning that if they lend with interest or defraud through dishonest weights, they will return to poverty and destitution. Accordingly, Hashem answers them: Remember that I am Hashem your God who brought you up from the land of Egypt, where you lived in poverty and lacked everything. If you continue weighing with deceitful scales, I will again make you dwell in tents as in the days of the appointed time. You will again become impoverished tent-dwellers, lacking any permanent house or dwelling, as you were during the appointed time of your departure from Egypt. Alternatively, because of your poverty and destitution, you will cease possessing livestock and property and conducting all commerce, just as commercial activity ceases on festivals and holy days.
text.11_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And I spoke through the prophets: I desired to bring them back through repentance, and therefore I provided them with many prophets. In the days of Ahab, several hundred prophets arose, all of whom were disciples of Elijah, and they addressed and rebuked the people. I also multiplied visions, another form of prophecy, for He communicated with the prophets both through speech and through visions, as well as through images and parables. Thus He says, and through the prophets I presented likenesses. But none of this was effective, for:
text.11_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: If Gilead is wicked, then they were surely in vain: It was already explained above (6:8) that all the prophets who were Elijah’s disciples were killed in Gilead, where Elijah had his residence. There Jezebel killed Hashem’s prophets, concerning which it says, “Gilead is a city of evildoers, tracked with blood.” Thus, if Gilead was filled with wickedness through the killing of the prophets, then surely these prophets existed in vain and to no purpose. For in response, they sacrificed bulls in Gilgal: corresponding to the number of the disciples of the prophets whom they killed, they sacrificed bulls to idols in Gilgal and erected altars to Baal—an altar and a bull as a burnt offering for every prophet they had murdered. Thus He says, their altars were also like heaps upon the furrows of the field, for they imagined that through these offerings they could appease the blood of the prophets that had been shed.
text.11_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Jacob fled, etc.; and through a prophet He brought up, etc.; Ephraim provoked Him bitterly: The meaning is that Ephraim responded with bitter provocation. When rebuked for the matters mentioned above—his falsehood and denial in worshiping the calves, and his deceit in possessing dishonest scales—he answers both accusations with mockery and derision, seeking to provoke those who rebuke him through bitter words. In response to the rebuke concerning deceit, he provocatively answers: Did not Jacob flee to the field of Aram? Jacob fled from Esau to the field of Aram because of deceit and trickery, for he had deceived Esau regarding the birthright and the blessing. Thus, Jacob too practiced deceit. Moreover, Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he tended sheep. While in Laban’s house, he first worked for a wife—Rachel—but Laban deceived him and gave him Leah. The deception remained effective, for Jacob then had to tend the sheep again for another wife and was compelled to labor for two wives. Thus, deceit had already been practiced since the days of our forefathers.
text.11_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And through a prophet: In response to the rebuke concerning their denial and the calves they had made, they claimed that they required an intermediary between themselves and Hashem. When Israel made the calf, they likewise said, “Make us a god, for as for this man Moses, who brought us up from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.” Moses had initially served as an intermediary between them and Hashem; when Moses disappeared from them, they made the calf to go before them and serve as an intermediary between them and Hashem. On this basis, they too claimed that they needed the calves as intermediaries through which they would receive Divine bounty. They offered as proof that through a prophet Hashem brought Israel up from the land of Egypt. Thus, even the Exodus from Egypt occurred through an intermediary—the prophet. Likewise, afterward, through a prophet Israel was preserved, for the prophet continually served as an intermediary in conveying Divine bounty. This demonstrates, they argued, that an intermediary is required to bring spiritual influence down into the world, and therefore they made the calves.
text.11_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Ephraim provoked Him bitterly: Through these mocking replies—words of ridicule that penetrate into the innermost chambers—they provoked those who rebuked them and mocked them with bitter taunts. And his blood: The meaning of the verse is: His master shall cast his blood upon him and return his disgrace to him. They killed their kings because of the sin of idolatry, as they killed the houses of Jeroboam and Ahab and other kings for this offense. Yet after killing them, they themselves returned to supporting the worship of Baal and the calves. Thus, they had murdered their kings without justification. The prophet therefore depicts his master—the murdered king—as rising from his grave and casting his blood upon him, placing the guilt for his blood, which had been shed without cause, upon the people who murdered him. And he returns his disgrace to him: The disgrace with which they taunted the king when they murdered him for practicing idolatry, he now returns upon them and casts back into their own bosom, reproaching them for the same offense. The prophet will now relate the words that their murdered master addresses to them:
text.12_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: When he spoke—his master shall return his disgrace to him: The murdered king addresses him, saying: When Ephraim spoke, it was from trembling. When Ephraim—that is, the king who belonged to the tribe of Ephraim—commanded the worship of the calves, he acted from trembling, fear, and anxiety. He was afraid because he had been elevated in Israel: due to his position as ruler, he feared that the people would go up to Jerusalem, return to their former master—the king of Judah—and kill him. Because of this fear, he commanded them to practice idolatry, as related concerning Jeroboam (I Kings 11). Yet although he acted under the pressure of fear and anxiety, nevertheless, he incurred guilt through Baal. This was still accounted to him as a sin, for which he deserved punishment, and he died—the people therefore killed him.
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And now: After murdering the king because of this guilt, how can they continue to sin? Their present sin is even greater than it was while the king remained alive, for now they make a molten image for themselves from their own silver, according to their own understanding. Until now, they had not made the molten image themselves; the king had made it. Now they make it themselves. Until now, it had not been made from their silver but from the king’s silver; now they make it from their own silver. Until now, it had not been fashioned according to their own understanding and judgment; now they make it according to their own conception. Is not their present sin therefore far greater? All this is the murdered king’s response to them.
text.12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: Idols: He continues with another sublime metaphor. He depicts the idols as entirely the work of craftsmen—that is, the idols were fashioned with such skill and artistry that they appear to possess mouths capable of speech. He therefore portrays the idols as speaking to them. When the people come to kiss and honor them, the idols say: “Shall those who sacrifice human beings kiss calves?” Those who sacrificed a human being—that is, who murdered the king because he worshiped the calves—how can they themselves now kiss those very calves? Since you have come to kiss the calves, it is evident that you sacrificed a human being and murdered him without cause.
text.12_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, they shall be like a morning cloud: Regarding the withholding of goodness and blessing from them, he says they will resemble a morning cloud that appears to promise rains of blessing but quickly dissipates and disappears. They will also be like dew that vanishes early: Even if they receive some measure of prosperity, it will not last but will resemble dew that forms during the night and disappears in the morning. Beyond withholding goodness, He will actively bring calamity upon them and send them into exile. At first, they will be like chaff blown from the threshing floor: The wind carries away the chaff while the grain remains; likewise, the wicked will be exiled while the righteous remain. Afterward, they will be like smoke blown from a chimney: Just as the wind carries all the smoke away, so He will ultimately exile them all.
text.12_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: But I am Hashem your God: This responds to their claim that Hashem does not watch over them directly and that they therefore require an intermediary between themselves and Him. As they said, “Through a prophet Hashem brought Israel up from Egypt,” they established the calves as intermediaries to convey Divine bounty. He answers them: Am I not Hashem your God since the land of Egypt? I Myself brought you out from there without any intermediary. At that time, you knew no god besides Me: There was no other god beside Me serving as a secondary power. Moreover, there was no savior besides Me: There was not even a savior acting as My emissary, for I Myself saved you without any intermediary.
text.12_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: I: And in the wilderness, after I brought you out of Egypt, I knew you through My Providence and care, supplying all your needs in a land of burning thirst, where you could survive only through continual miracles—the manna, the well, and the pillar of cloud—all of which came solely from Me, for miracles come from God alone.
text.12_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: When they had pasture: Only after I brought them from the wilderness into an inhabited land did they find pasture and become satisfied. Because they were satisfied, their heart became exalted; therefore, they forgot Me, as it says, “Then your heart will become exalted, and you will forget Hashem your God.”
text.12_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And I became to them like a lion: They forgot God’s goodness and denied the benefits He had bestowed upon them, yet they attributed the calamities that befell them to Hashem, until He appeared in their eyes like a savage beast that tears its prey—a lion, leopard, bear, and lioness. These four animals correspond to the four kingdoms that destroyed them. The lion represents the kingdoms of Babylon and Assyria, for Daniel saw that “the first was like a lion,” as explained above concerning the verse, “He shall roar like a lion.” The leopard represents the kingdom of Greece. Thus He says, like a leopard I will watch along the road, for Greece came by way of the Land of Israel but did not exile them from their land, as it says, “A leopard watches over their cities.”
text.12_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: I will encounter them like a bereaved bear: This corresponds to the second beast Daniel saw, which “resembled a bear,” representing the kingdom of Media. Then I will tear open the enclosure of their heart—in the days of Haman, when they opened their hearts and returned in repentance. And there I will devour them like a lioness: This refers to the exile of Edom, represented by the fourth beast, which “devoured and crushed, and trampled the remainder with its feet.” That is, throughout all these exiles, they imagined that I was the One tearing them apart. In truth, however, this is mistaken, for the beast of the field shall rend them. Because I concealed My face from them, the beasts of the field came upon them and tore them apart.
text.12_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Your destruction, O Israel: Your destruction by the kings and the Almighty is not My doing. Rather, you have destroyed yourself: by corrupting your own way, you bring destruction upon yourself and become your own destroyer.
text.12_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: For in Me: You imagine that your destruction depends upon Me only because I had been your help. Therefore, when I began to conceal My face from you and ceased assisting you, you were destroyed. I caused this only passively, by withholding My help—not actively, by bringing about your destruction.
text.12_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Shall I be your king? Your destruction resulted from having no king, for by rebelling against Hoshea and denouncing him to the king of Assyria, they brought destruction upon themselves (as explained above, chapter 10). He therefore says: Shall I now serve as your king and protect you from the king of Assyria? Where is the one who will save you in all your cities? The meaning is: Search throughout all your cities and among all your judges—where can a king be found who will save you?
text.12_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: Concerning whom you said, “Give me a king and princes”: In ancient times, during the period of the Judges, Hashem was their King, leading and delivering them, as in the days of Samuel. They then assembled and demanded a human king because they rejected the Kingdom of Heaven, as Samuel reproached them. Hashem told him, “It is not you whom they have rejected, but Me whom they have rejected from reigning over them.” Initially, they lived under Hashem’s Providence above the natural order, but they requested to be governed according to the ways of nature, as I explained there at length. He therefore says: How can you now ask Me to be your king? You rejected My kingship and chose a human king to save you through warfare, saying, “Give me a king and princes.” Where, then, is that king who will save you?
text.12_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: I gave: When I gave you a king in the days of Samuel, it was in My anger, for I knew that you would ultimately divide into separate kingdoms and worship the calves. Thus, this was not according to My desire.
text.12_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: And I took him away in My wrath: Hoshea, the final king, was better than the kings who preceded him and did not deserve punishment on account of his own deeds. He was removed only because of the general overflowing wrath: because My wrath extended over the people as a whole—which is the defining meaning of the term evrah—I took him away from you, even though My anger did not burn against him personally.
text.12_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Bound up: Ephraim does not abandon his transgressions. Rather, his iniquity is bound up with him, and his sin is stored away. He carefully preserves them and refuses to relinquish them and return in repentance.
text.12_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: The pangs of a woman in labor shall come upon him: He compares the afflictions and anguish that befell the nation to the pangs of a woman giving birth. The more intense and frequent the labor pains become, the greater the hope that she will soon deliver the child from her full womb and that the pains will cease. He already used this metaphor in Isaiah 37:3: “Children have come to the birth opening, but there is no strength to give birth.” This means that because of the abundance of labor pains, it appears that the children within her womb have reached the birth opening and are close to being born, but the mother lacks the strength to expel them from her womb and deliver them. In the allegory, their afflictions and anguish have become so great that the time appears to have arrived for the nation’s children to emerge from distress and be born as a people saved by Hashem, which represents the nation’s birth. Yet the mother lacks the inner strength by which nature expels the fetus—meaning that the nation lacks the commandments and good deeds through which the people could be born as children of the living God. Here he says figuratively that although the nation has experienced the pangs of childbirth, the child within the womb is not wise like other children, who possess the wisdom to emerge from the womb at the time of delivery and reach the birth opening, where children stand at birth and through which they are delivered into the world. Thus He says, he is an unwise son, for when the time arrives—although the moment of birth has arrived and he should emerge, reach the birth opening, and be born—he does not stand at the birth opening, where children are born and emerge from the womb. Because he lacks wisdom, he does not understand that he must emerge at the time of birth and reach the birth opening, but remains like a stillborn child within his mother’s womb. The allegory is that the time had arrived for the nation to be reborn and renewed, for its many afflictions had already brought upon it the pangs of labor. Yet they did not reach the birth opening—that is, they did not repent, which is the path to rebirth. He therefore prefaced this with the statement, “Ephraim’s iniquity is bound up,” depicting iniquity as harmful fluids confined within a full womb that prevent the child from being born. Likewise, the iniquity and sin bound up and stored within them prevented them from repenting and being reborn, although they resembled a pregnant woman approaching delivery, crying out in the anguish of her labor.
text.12_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: From the hand: He explains the statement that the time had arrived for them to be born. I had thought that I would redeem them from the power of the graveand rescue them from death. The grave represents exile, while death represents the slaughter inflicted upon them. Hashem intended to save them both from exile from their land and from widespread killing, through which they would be born anew. But they did not reach the birth opening and did not repent. Therefore, I will become your plague, O death. He turns toward death and the grave and addresses them directly: Not only will I no longer redeem them from your hand, but from now on I Myself will become your plague, O death—the agent you send to put them to death. That is, I will become your emissary to kill and destroy them.
text.12_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: And I will become your destruction, O grave: O grave, I Myself will become your bitter destroying force through which you consume people. That is, I will serve as your agent in exiling them. Not only will I refrain from redeeming them because they did not repent; I will also consume them through death, exile them from their land through My Providence, and actively assist in bringing this about. Compassion shall be hidden from My eyes: The term here denotes relenting and regret, which ordinarily cause an adverse decree to be withdrawn and anger to subside. When the people regret their deeds and return in repentance, Hashem relents from the calamity He had declared He would bring. But now relenting will remain hidden and will not come before My eyes, for the people do not regret or repent of their deeds, and therefore I will not relent from the calamity.
text.12_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: For it bears fruit only among brothers: This refers to relenting. Relenting can bear fruit only among brothers—when Israel acts fraternally and unites with one another. Only then would relenting be possible. It was already explained that in the days of Hoshea son of Elah, the worship of the calves was abandoned, and the barriers Jeroboam had established to prevent Israel from making the pilgrimage to Jerusalem were abolished. Yet certain factions opposed Hoshea for this reason and denounced him to the king of Assyria (as explained above, 8:4; 10:2, 7). Likewise, II Chronicles 30 relates that Hezekiah sent messengers to the tribes urging them to return to Hashem. Some mocked the messengers, while others humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem. Thus, two opposing factions existed among them at that time. Consequently, relenting did not bear its fruit there, and the entire people did not repent; therefore, Hashem did not relent from the calamity. As a result, an east wind shall come—the king of Assyria, who came against them from the east, beyond the Jordan, traveling through the wilderness. He is Hashem’s wind, rising from the wilderness, for Hashem sent him against them. His spring shall dry up: The Assyrian king devastated the land that had been Israel’s source. Consequently, his fountain shall become parched: The fountain flowing from that source will dry up, for Israel will be scattered to the four corners of the heavens, and the waters of its abundance, continued existence, and prosperity will cease. He shall plunder the treasury: This wind will also plunder all their treasures and every precious vessel. They have no further hope, for they have been lost and banished because of their sin.
text.13_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Samaria shall bear her guilt: When the seer heard that there would be no relenting and that Hashem would not revoke the irrevocable decree, he turned toward Israel as a whole. He said to them: The principal offender in rebellion and treachery was Samaria, the royal city, whose inhabitants upheld the worship of the calves and caused all Israel to stumble. Israel itself stumbled only because the kings of Samaria led the people astray. Thus, Israel still possesses the possibility of repentance. Why, then, should all Israel perish together with Samaria? I therefore say that Samaria should bear her own guilt—she should carry the blame, for she rebelled against her God through willful defiance and revolt. It is fitting that she be punished until her inhabitants fall by the sword and their infants are dashed to pieces. According to strict justice, they deserve this punishment because they have no possibility of correction. But:
text.13_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Return, O Israel: But you, Israel—the people as a whole apart from Samaria—can still return in repentance, for you have stumbled through your iniquity. You did not sin through willful defiance and rebellion; rather, you stumbled because those who led you—the kings of Samaria—caused you to stumble. You were therefore like one who sins unintentionally or under compulsion, and you can still be restored. At first, he says, Return as far as Hashem. The word ad, “as far as,” indicates that Hashem stands at a distance from them and that they must travel toward Him until they reach the place where He is. That is, they must abandon their former sins, regret having previously strayed from the path through error or compulsion, and seek the path by which to return all the way to Hashem.
text.13_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Take: He adds that after you have reached Hashem and drawn near to Him, you should continue improving your conduct for the future and repent out of love, until you take words with you—meaning things that will speak on your behalf, argue your case favorably, and testify to your merit: the commandments and good deeds you perform. And return a second time to Hashem. This is repentance motivated by love, through which deliberate sins are reckoned not merely as unintentional offenses but as merits. Forgiveness will then no longer be granted because their sins are regarded as having been committed under compulsion, unintentionally, or through error. Rather, forgiveness will result from the merits and righteous deeds they bring with them to argue in their favor. Through these, He will forgive them even if their original sins are considered deliberate, for He will see that after rebelling against Him, they returned to love and serve Him wholeheartedly—not from fear of punishment, but from love. Then say to Him, “Forgive all iniquity and accept what is good.” First, forgive all iniquity—not as before, when He did not remove the entire sin but only part of it, since an unintentional offense still remained and He removed only the aspect considered deliberate. Now, forgive it even when it is regarded as deliberate iniquity, and nevertheless pardon them. This will occur because You accept what is good—You place against it the goodness of their deeds and merits. This also accords with the teaching of our Sages that the sin itself is transformed into merit, so that the iniquities become merits and the evil itself is transformed into good.
text.13_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: And let our lips substitute for bulls: At first, when He did not remove the entire iniquity but regarded it merely as an unintentional stumbling, they still remained obligated to bring bulls as sacrifices for the inadvertent sin. For when the community sins because of an erroneous legal ruling, it must bring a bull as a sin offering for each tribe. But now that You will remove even the unintentional aspect of the sin, the words spoken by our lips will take the place of the bulls formerly required as sin offerings. He now explains what words they will utter with their lips.
text.13_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Assyria: We will declare to You with our lips that from now on we will place our trust in nothing besides You. We will not trust in Assyria, upon whom the kings of Israel relied in their distress, for Assyria will not save us. Nor will we trust in Egypt, which supplied us with horses and chariots so that we might fight through our own strength, for we will not ride upon horses. We will no longer trust in idols or the celestial order, for we will no longer call the work of our hands “our God.” We will trust in You alone, because we know that in You the orphan finds compassion. One who possesses no natural helper or support receives compassion from You because of Your mercy. Likewise, once we place our confidence and hope in nothing else, we will find compassion with You.
text.13_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: I will heal: Hashem answers them: First, I will heal their backsliding. He compares their rebelliousness to a wound clinging to them, which He will heal; through repentance, they will recover from their affliction. Afterward, I will love them freely—I will return to loving them. Not only will I forgive their past, but I will love them, and I will do this from the generosity of My heart, for My anger has turned away from him—that is, from his backsliding. Until now, My anger burned because of their backsliding; once My anger turns away, I will return to loving them.
text.13_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: I will be like dew to Israel; he shall blossom like a rose: Naturalists have described a flower called the Rose of Jericho, which is not rooted in the ground. The wind carries it through deserts to distant lands, where it is moistened by dew and blossoms and grows in beauty and splendor. This serves as a metaphor for Israel, carried by the wind from place to place, exiled and wandering. Hashem is the dew that preserves Israel’s life during exile, enabling it to blossom in beauty and splendor like a rose.
text.13_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: Though He struck his roots like Lebanon: Although He struck the roots that had formerly been planted firmly in their land like the trees of Lebanon—for cedars take root deep within the ground—those roots were struck and uprooted from their place, leaving Israel without roots or any permanent dwelling. Nevertheless, although the roots were struck—
text.13_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: His shoots shall spread: The tender branches that emerge from the ground beside the roots will extend and spread outward. That is, the children living at the End of Days—the new shoots that arise after the former roots were struck and destroyed—will become flourishing, fruit-bearing trees. His splendor shall be like the olive tree: Just as the olive produces oil for illumination, so their fruit will shine with Hashem’s light. The olive’s leaves remain fresh in both summer and winter; likewise, their prosperity will endure in every season. And his fragrance shall be like Lebanon: They will again possess the fragrance of Lebanon—holiness and purity associated with Lebanon, which is in the Land of Israel, the place of purity and holiness.
text.13_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: They shall return: From among them, those who desire to become dwellers in his shade—that is, in the shade of Lebanon—will return. He prophesies that many of the exiles will return to dwell in the Land of Israel and establish their homes in the holy land beneath Lebanon’s shade. There they shall revive the grain, possessing grain with which to provide bread for their households.
text.13_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: And they shall blossom like a vine that spreads far and wide, for they will multiply and flourish there, producing fruit and abundant yield.
text.13_Chapter, 7_Verse, 2_Comment: Its remembrance: The remembrance of Lebanon will be like the wine of Lebanon. Even those who do not return to dwell beneath Lebanon’s shade and reside in the Land of Israel will continually remember Lebanon, just as one remembers the exceptionally fine wine of Lebanon, whose memory never leaves the heart of the person who drinks it. Likewise, they will remember “the good mountain and Lebanon” in all their prayers and elevate Jerusalem above their greatest joy.
text.13_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Ephraim: Even Ephraim, who formerly practiced idolatry, will then say, “What have I to do any longer with idols?” He will recognize that they possess no reality or power.
text.13_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: I have answered him and will watch over him: I will then answer their prayers and watch over them from afar through My Providence. He explains what He will answer them: I am like a flourishing cypress. I resemble a cypress whose many branches spread outward and whose leaves remain perpetually fresh, so that one sitting beneath it finds shelter from the sun’s heat and protection from torrents and rain. Likewise, one who takes refuge in Me will find protection from every adversity at every time and in every season. Do not imagine, however, that I resemble a cypress that bears no fruit, for from Me your fruit is found. Whatever fruit you possess comes from Me—that is, I bestow both material and spiritual goodness. My fruit is the fruit of the Tree of Life.
text.13_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Who is wise? Wisdom consists of received teachings, whereas understanding is the ability to derive one thing from another. Through his understanding, a person can reach conclusions even concerning matters for which he possesses no tradition from his teachers. Such are the rational deductions a person draws from propositions based upon first principles and sensory experience. But regarding matters inaccessible to unaided reason—such as Hashem’s governance and Providence and all matters concerning Divinity—a person cannot understand them through his intellect unless he first possesses received premises transmitted through the paths of wisdom, such as the foundations of Torah and faith received from the prophets. He can then derive one thing from another on the basis of what he has received through the principles of wisdom. Thus He says, Who is wise and will understand these things? I have already explained elsewhere that the principles of wisdom are not established by demonstrative proofs. Knowledge, by definition, concerns something of which a person possesses clear awareness, such as matters apprehended through his senses. A person does not know the principles of wisdom independently. Only one who possesses understanding and investigates the principles of wisdom by deriving one thing from another will ultimately attain knowledge of them with clear certainty. Therefore, He says, Who possesses understanding and will know them? This is because the ways of Hashem are upright. People complain about Divine Providence when they see a righteous person suffering and a wicked person prospering. This appears to us as disorder in the Divine governance and seems to indicate that there is neither Providence nor reward and punishment. But one who has received the principles of wisdom—that Hashem exercises Providence and that His ways are goodness, kindness, and compassion—will understand and know that Hashem’s ways are intrinsically upright. The apparent disorder arises from those who are governed: transgressors stumble upon them because they fail to direct their steps properly along the upright path. The defect is not in the path but in those walking upon it, who do not straighten their steps to follow the ways of uprightness. But the righteous shall walk in them without stumbling. He says this in response to those who complain about the exile and Hashem’s punishments of His people, which make it appear as though He has abandoned them to chance and lawlessness. The wise and understanding, however, will know that everything occurs through Divine Providence and that the ways of Hashem are upright, for He is righteous and just.
